title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
1.1 Problem 1: Historical Short-Rate Volatility
Weekly short-rate changes, in basis points, are
\[2,\;-2,\;4,\;-1,\;3,\;-3,\;5,\;0.\]

Compute the sample mean.

Compute the sample weekly standard deviation.

Annualize the standard deviation using \(\sqrt{52}\).

Interpret the annualized result and identify one limitation.







NoteSolution





There are eight observations. Their sum is 8 bps, so
\[\bar{x}=\frac{8}{8}=\boxed{1.00\text{ bp per week}}.\]
The deviations from the mean are \(1,-3,3,-2,2,-4,4,-1\). Their squared deviations sum to
\[1+9+9+4+4+16+16+1=60.\]
Using the sample denominator \(n-1=7\),
\[s=\sqrt{\frac{60}{7}}=\boxed{2.9277\text{ bps per week}}.\]
The square-root-of-time annualization is
\[s_{\text{annual}}=2.9277\sqrt{52}=\boxed{21.11\text{ bps per year}}.\]
This describes the annualized scale of short-rate changes if weekly changes are independent and have stable variance. Those assumptions may fail when volatility clusters or the monetary-policy regime changes.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 1.2 Problem 2: Mean Reversion and a One-Standard-Deviation Shock
text:
1.2 Problem 2: Mean Reversion and a One-Standard-Deviation Shock
The short rate follows the Euler approximation
\[\Delta r=a(\theta-r)\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\varepsilon,\]
where \(r=5.00\%\), \(\theta=3.50\%\), \(a=0.80\), \(\sigma=1.20\%\) per year, \(\Delta t=0.25\), and \(E[\varepsilon]=0\).

Compute the expected quarterly rate change.

Compute the expected rate after one quarter.

Compute the standard deviation of the quarterly shock.

Give the rates corresponding to shocks of \(\varepsilon=+1\) and \(-1\).







NoteSolution





The expected shock is zero. The mean-reversion component is
\[E[\Delta r]=0.80(0.035-0.050)(0.25)=-0.0030=-30\text{ bps}.\]
Therefore,
\[E[r_{t+0.25}]=0.0500-0.0030=\boxed{4.70\%}.\]
The shock standard deviation is
\[\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}=0.012\sqrt{0.25}=0.0060=60\text{ bps}.\]
For \(\varepsilon=+1\), the rate is \(4.70\%+0.60\%=\boxed{5.30\%}\); for \(\varepsilon=-1\), it is \(4.70\%-0.60\%=\boxed{4.10\%}\). Mean reversion controls the center of the distribution, while \(\sigma\) controls its dispersion.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 1.3 Problem 3: Nodes in a Lognormal Short-Rate Tree
text:
1.3 Problem 3: Nodes in a Lognormal Short-Rate Tree
A model specifies year-2 short rates as
\[r_{2,j}=a_2e^{(2j-2)\sigma},\qquad j=0,1,2,\]
with \(a_2=4.00\%\) and \(\sigma=0.15\).

Compute all three year-2 short rates.

Compute the one-year discount factor \(1/(1+r)\) at each node.

Which parameter sets the middle level of the rates?

If \(\sigma\) rises while \(a_2\) is unchanged, what happens numerically to the distance between the low and high nodes?







NoteSolution





For \(j=0,1,2\), the exponents are \(-0.30,0,+0.30\). Thus,
\[
\begin{aligned}
r_{2,0}&=0.04e^{-0.30}=\boxed{2.9633\%},\\
r_{2,1}&=0.04=\boxed{4.0000\%},\\
r_{2,2}&=0.04e^{0.30}=\boxed{5.3994\%}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The associated one-year discount factors are approximately
\[\boxed{0.9712,\quad 0.9615,\quad 0.9488}.\]
The level parameter \(a_2\) fixes the middle node. The current low-to-high distance is \(5.3994\%-2.9633\%=2.4361\%\). A larger \(\sigma\) lowers the low node and raises the high node, widening this distance; this is how volatility controls dispersion.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
1.4 Problem 4: A One-Period Bond-Option Tree
One year from today, a zero-coupon bond will be worth either 94 in the up-rate state or 98 in the down-rate state. A European call expiring then has strike 96. The risk-neutral probability of the up-rate state is 0.55, and today’s one-year short rate is 4%.

Compute the call payoff in each state.

Compute the call’s time-0 value.

Compute the hedge ratio \((C_d-C_u)/(B_d-B_u)\).

Explain why the call pays more in the down-rate state.







NoteSolution





The payoffs are
\[C_u=\max(94-96,0)=0,\qquad C_d=\max(98-96,0)=2.\]
Risk-neutral valuation gives
\[C_0=\frac{0.55(0)+0.45(2)}{1.04}=\boxed{0.8654}.\]
The option changes by 2 when the bond changes by 4, so
\[h=\frac{2-0}{98-94}=\boxed{0.50}.\]
When rates fall, discount factors rise and the zero-coupon bond price is higher. The call is therefore in the money in the down-rate state.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
2.1 Problem 5: Estimating a Static Spread
A corporate bond trades at 101.00. Discounting its promised cash flows at Treasury zero rates plus a trial spread gives:



Spread
Model value




40 bps
101.40


60 bps
100.72




Explain why the value falls as the spread rises.

Estimate the static spread by linear interpolation.

How far is the estimate from each trial spread?

State what risk the static spread does not model for a callable bond.







NoteSolution





A larger spread raises every discount rate, reducing present value. Since 101.00 lies between the two trial values, the spread lies between 40 and 60 bps:
\[
s\approx40+
\frac{101.40-101.00}{101.40-100.72}(60-40)
=\boxed{51.76\text{ bps}}.
\]
It is 11.76 bps above 40 and 8.24 bps below 60. Interpolation is an approximation because price is convex rather than perfectly linear in spread. A static spread also ignores the path-dependent exercise of an embedded call; OAS uses a rate lattice to model that behavior.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
2.2 Problem 6: Pricing a Callable Bond
A two-year annual-pay bond has face value 100 and coupon 6. The time-0 short rate is 5%. At year 1, rates are either 4% or 8%, each with risk-neutral probability 0.5. The bond may be called at 101 at year 1, after the continuation value is calculated. Coupons are added after discounting the next payment.

Compute the year-2 payment.

Compute the year-1 option-free hold value at each node.

Apply the call rule and compute the time-0 callable value.

Compute the option-free value and the embedded call value.







NoteSolution





The maturity payment is \(100+6=106\). The year-1 hold values are
\[V_{1,L}=\frac{106}{1.04}+6=107.9231,\]
\[V_{1,H}=\frac{106}{1.08}+6=104.1481.\]
Both exceed the call price, so the issuer calls in both states and the ex-coupon node value is capped at 101. The callable value is
\[V_0^{\text{call}}=\frac{0.5(101)+0.5(101)}{1.05}+6
=\boxed{102.1905}.\]
Without the call,
\[V_0^{\text{straight}}
=\frac{0.5(107.9231)+0.5(104.1481)}{1.05}+6
=\boxed{106.9863}.\]
Thus, the issuer’s embedded call is worth
\[106.9863-102.1905=\boxed{4.7958}\]
to the issuer and reduces the value received by the investor by the same amount.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
2.3 Problem 7: Pricing a Putable Bond
A two-year annual-pay bond has face value 100 and coupon 3. The time-0 short rate is 5%. At year 1, rates are either 3% or 10%, each with probability 0.5. The investor may put the bond at 100 at year 1.

Compute the year-2 payment.

Compute the year-1 hold values.

Apply the put rule.

Compute the time-0 putable and option-free values and the embedded put value.







NoteSolution





The maturity payment is \(100+3=103\). The hold values are
\[V_{1,L}=\frac{103}{1.03}+3=103.0000,\]
\[V_{1,H}=\frac{103}{1.10}+3=96.6364.\]
The investor keeps the bond in the low-rate state and exercises the put in the high-rate state. Hence the year-1 values are 103 and 100. The time-0 putable value is
\[V_0^{\text{put}}=\frac{0.5(103)+0.5(100)}{1.05}+3
=\boxed{99.6667}.\]
The option-free value is
\[V_0^{\text{straight}}
=\frac{0.5(103)+0.5(96.6364)}{1.05}+3
=\boxed{98.0649}.\]
The embedded investor put is worth
\[99.6667-98.0649=\boxed{1.6017}.\]

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 2.4 Problem 8: OAS, Effective Duration, and Convexity
text:
2.4 Problem 8: OAS, Effective Duration, and Convexity
A callable bond has market price \(P_0=100.00\). Trial OAS prices are 100.40 at 45 bps and 99.95 at 60 bps. After solving for OAS, the model gives \(P_-=102.60\) when the curve falls 50 bps and \(P_+=97.70\) when it rises 50 bps.

Estimate the OAS.

Compute effective duration.

Compute effective convexity.

Interpret the two measures.







NoteSolution





Interpolating to the market price,
\[\text{OAS}\approx45+
\frac{100.40-100.00}{100.40-99.95}(60-45)
=\boxed{58.33\text{ bps}}.\]
With \(\Delta y=0.005\),
\[D_{\text{eff}}=\frac{P_--P_+}{2P_0\Delta y}
=\frac{102.60-97.70}{2(100)(0.005)}=\boxed{4.90}.\]
\[C_{\text{eff}}=\frac{P_-+P_+-2P_0}{P_0(\Delta y)^2}
=\frac{102.60+97.70-200}{100(0.005)^2}=\boxed{120.00}.\]
Effective duration measures the local price slope after allowing the call decision to change. Effective convexity measures curvature under the same full repricing; both are therefore preferable to cash-flow duration for an option-embedded bond.

section: 3.1 Problem 9: Treasury Futures Quotation and Margin Cash Flows
text:
3.1 Problem 9: Treasury Futures Quotation and Margin Cash Flows
A trader buys one Treasury futures contract at 101-12. Subsequent settlements are 101-20, 101-08, and 101-24. Quotes are in 32nds, and one point is worth \(\$1,000\).

Convert all four prices to decimals.

Compute each daily cash flow to the long.

Compute cumulative profit or loss.

Explain the sign of the cash flows.







NoteSolution





The decimal prices are
\[101.375,\quad 101.625,\quad 101.250,\quad 101.750.\]
Daily marking to market gives

Price change
Long cash flow

\(+0.250\)
\(+\$250\)


2
\(-0.375\)

\(+0.500\)

The cumulative result is \(250-375+500=\boxed{\$375}\), equal to \((101.750-101.375)(\$1{,}000)\). A long receives cash when the settlement price rises and pays cash when it falls.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
3.2 Problem 10: Three-Month SOFR Futures
A long Three-Month SOFR futures position moves from 95.18 to 95.26. Each one-basis- point price move is worth \(\$25\) per contract.

Compute both implied SOFR rates.

Compute the price move in basis points.

Compute the long’s dollar gain or loss.

Explain the inverse price-rate relation.







NoteSolution





The quoted rate is \(100-\) futures price. Initially it is \(100-95.18=\boxed{4.82\%}\) and afterward it is \(100-95.26=\boxed{4.74\%}\). The price rose by 0.08, or 8 basis points, so the long earns
\[8(\$25)=\boxed{\$200}.\]
The contract is quoted as 100 minus the implied rate; therefore, an increase in price mechanically corresponds to a decrease in the implied rate.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 3.4 Problem 12: Futures DV01 and a Portfolio Hedge
text:
3.4 Problem 12: Futures DV01 and a Portfolio Hedge
Using Bond C from Problem 11, assume modified duration 7.10, clean price 106.40, deliverable face value \(\$100,000\), and conversion factor 0.9450. A long bond portfolio has DV01 of \(\$30,500\).

Compute the CTD market value.

Compute CTD DV01.

Compute approximate futures DV01.

Compute the contract hedge and state its direction.







NoteSolution





The deliverable market value is
\[MV_{CTD}=1.0640(\$100{,}000)=\$106{,}400.\]
Therefore,
\[DV01_{CTD}=7.10(\$106{,}400)(0.0001)=\boxed{\$75.5440}.\]
Adjusting for the conversion factor,
\[DV01_F\approx\frac{75.5440}{0.9450}=\boxed{\$79.9407}.\]
The hedge requires
\[N=\frac{30{,}500}{79.9407}=381.53.\]
The manager should sell approximately \(\boxed{382}\) futures contracts because the long bond portfolio loses when rates rise, while short futures gain. Rounding to a whole contract leaves a small residual DV01.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
4.1 Problem 13: Spread Duration and DTS
A corporate bond position has market value \(\$5,000,000\), spread duration 4.20, and spread 220 bps. Its spread widens by 30 bps.

Estimate the percentage price change.

Estimate the dollar change.

Compute DTS using spread in percentage points.

Interpret DTS.







NoteSolution





Using \(\Delta P/P\approx-SD\,\Delta s\) and \(\Delta s=0.0030\),
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-4.20(0.0030)=\boxed{-1.26\%}.\]
The dollar change is
\[-0.0126(\$5{,}000{,}000)=\boxed{-\$63{,}000}.\]
With spread expressed as 2.20 percentage points,
\[DTS=4.20(2.20)=\boxed{9.24}.\]
Equivalently, using decimal spread gives 0.0924. DTS combines sensitivity and the current spread level, providing a rough relative measure of spread risk across bonds with different credit quality.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
4.2 Problem 14: Empirical Duration Multiplier
A \(\$20\) million corporate bond position has analytical duration 6.50 and spread \(s=2.50\%=0.025\). The correlation between Treasury-yield changes and relative spread changes is \(-0.60\). Their volatilities are \(\sigma_y=0.25\%\) and \(\sigma_s=2.00\%\).

Compute \(\beta=\rho\sigma_s/\sigma_y\).

Compute \(M=1+s\beta\) and empirical duration.

Estimate the loss for a 50 bp Treasury-yield increase.

Compare it with the analytical-duration loss.







NoteSolution





\[\beta=-0.60\frac{0.0200}{0.0025}=\boxed{-4.80}.\]
The duration multiplier and empirical duration are
\[M=1+0.025(-4.80)=\boxed{0.88},\]
\[D_{emp}=6.50(0.88)=\boxed{5.72}.\]
For \(\Delta y=0.0050\), the empirical estimate is
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-5.72(0.005)=-2.86\%,\]
\[\Delta P=-0.0286(\$20{,}000{,}000)=\boxed{-\$572{,}000}.\]
Analytical duration gives \(-6.50(0.005)=-3.25\%\), or \(-\$650,000\). It overstates this empirically adjusted loss by \(\boxed{\$78,000}\) because spreads are assumed to tighten when Treasury yields rise.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 4.3 Problem 15: A One-Period Structural Credit Model
text:
4.3 Problem 15: A One-Period Structural Credit Model
A firm owes \(\$100\) million in one year. Its asset value will be \(\$140\) million with probability 0.65 or \(\$70\) million with probability 0.35. Ignore discounting.

Identify the default state.

Compute debt and equity payoffs in each state.

Compute expected debt and equity payoffs.

Compute expected debt loss and recovery in the default state.







NoteSolution





Default occurs when assets are below promised debt, so it occurs in the \(\$70\) million state.








Asset value
Debt payoff \(\min(V_A,100)\)
Equity payoff \(\max(V_A-100,0)\)




\(\$140m\)
\(\$100m\)
\(\$40m\)


\(\$70m\)
\(\$70m\)
\(0\)



Expected payoffs are
\[E[D]=0.65(100)+0.35(70)=\boxed{\$89.5\text{m}},\]
\[E[E]=0.65(40)+0.35(0)=\boxed{\$26.0\text{m}}.\]
Expected debt loss relative to the promised \(\$100\) million is \(\$10.5\) million. Recovery conditional on default is \(70/100=\boxed{70\%}\), so loss given default is 30%. Equity is a call option on firm assets with strike equal to debt face value.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 4.4 Problem 16: Default Intensity and Credit Spread
text:
4.4 Problem 16: Default Intensity and Credit Spread
A reduced-form model has constant annual intensity \(\lambda=2.5\%\) and loss given default of 60%.

Compute one-year survival and default probabilities.

Compute five-year survival and cumulative default probabilities.

For 100 surviving issuers, compute expected defaults during the next year.

Estimate the credit spread using \(s\approx\lambda\times LGD\).







NoteSolution





For constant intensity, \(S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\). At one year,
\[S(1)=e^{-0.025}=0.97531,\]
\[PD(1)=1-S(1)=\boxed{2.4690\%}.\]
At five years,
\[S(5)=e^{-0.125}=\boxed{88.2497\%},\]
\[PD(5)=1-S(5)=\boxed{11.7503\%}.\]
Among 100 initially surviving issuers, expected one-year defaults are \(100(0.024690)=\boxed{2.469}\). The spread approximation is
\[s\approx0.025(0.60)=0.0150=\boxed{150\text{ bps}}.\]
An observed spread may differ because it also reflects liquidity, risk premia, taxes, and uncertainty about recovery and intensity.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
5.1 Problem 17: Treasury Futures Put Quotation
A trader buys one 110 Treasury futures put for 0-48. Option premiums are quoted in 64ths, and one point is worth \(\$1,000\).

Convert the premium to points and dollars.

Compute the expiration break-even price in decimal and fractional notation.

Compute payoff and net profit if futures finish at 107-32.

Compute payoff and net profit if futures finish at 112-00.







NoteSolution





The quote means 48/64 of one point:
\[0\text{-}48=\frac{48}{64}=0.75\text{ point},\]
so the premium is \(0.75(\$1,000)=\boxed{\$750}\). Break-even for a long put is
\[K-p=110-0.75=109.25=\boxed{109\text{-}16},\]
because \(0.25=16/64\). At 107-32, \(F_T=107.50\), so
\[\text{payoff}=110-107.50=2.50\text{ points}=\$2,500,\]
\[\text{net profit}=2,500-750=\boxed{\$1,750}.\]
At 112-00 the put is out of the money, payoff is zero, and net profit is \(\boxed{-\$750}\). It should not be exercised.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 5.2 Problem 18: Put-Call Parity for Futures Options
text:
5.2 Problem 18: Put-Call Parity for Futures Options
European futures options have \(F_0=112\), \(K=110\), \(r=4\%\), \(T=0.5\), and call premium \(c=3.10\) points.

Compute \(e^{-rT}\).

Use \(c-p=e^{-rT}(F_0-K)\) to compute the fair put.

If the market put is 1.40, compute the mispricing in points and dollars.

Describe an arbitrage that locks in the difference.







NoteSolution





\[e^{-rT}=e^{-0.04(0.5)}=\boxed{0.980199}.\]
Therefore,
\[p=c-e^{-rT}(F_0-K)
=3.10-0.980199(2)=\boxed{1.1396\text{ points}}.\]
The market put at 1.40 is overpriced by
\[1.40-1.1396=0.2604\text{ point}=\boxed{\$260.40}.\]
At market prices, a long call and short put cost \(3.10-1.40=1.70\) points and have expiration payoff \(F_T-K\). Add a short futures contract, whose payoff is \(F_0-F_T\), and the combined expiration payoff is the certain amount \(F_0-K=2\). Borrow its present value, \(1.9604\), to finance the \(1.70\) option cost. The time-0 surplus is \(1.9604-1.70=0.2604\) point, while the expiration cash flows repay the borrowing.

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
section: 5.3 Problem 19: Black-Scholes on a Zero-Coupon Bond
text:
5.3 Problem 19: Black-Scholes on a Zero-Coupon Bond
A European call and put are written on a zero-coupon bond with \(S_0=95\), \(K=94\), \(T=0.75\), \(r=3\%\), and bond-price volatility \(\sigma=12\%\).

Compute \(\sigma\sqrt{T}\), \(d_1\), and \(d_2\).

Use \(N(d_1)=0.6444\) and \(N(d_2)=0.6050\) to compute the call.

Compute the put using complementary normal probabilities.

Verify put-call parity.







NoteSolution





\[\sigma\sqrt{T}=0.12\sqrt{0.75}=\boxed{0.103923}.\]
\[d_1=\frac{\ln(95/94)+(0.03+0.5(0.12)^2)(0.75)}{0.103923}
=\boxed{0.3703},\]
\[d_2=d_1-0.103923=\boxed{0.2664}.\]
The call value is
\[c=95(0.6444)-94e^{-0.03(0.75)}(0.6050)=\boxed{5.61}.\]
Using \(N(-d_1)=0.3556\) and \(N(-d_2)=0.3950\),
\[p=94e^{-0.0225}(0.3950)-95(0.3556)=\boxed{2.52}.\]
The values satisfy parity up to rounding:
\[c-p\approx5.61-2.52=3.09,\]
\[S_0-Ke^{-rT}=95-94e^{-0.0225}=3.09.\]

title: Practice Problems 2: Lectures 7–11
text:
5.4 Problem 20: Delta-DV01 Protective Put Hedge
A \(\$12\) million bond portfolio has modified duration 7.50. A Treasury futures contract has DV01 \(\$75\), current price 112, and point value \(\$1,000\). A put has strike 111, premium 1.10 points, and delta \(-0.45\).

Compute portfolio DV01 and futures-equivalent contracts.

Compute the number of puts for an initial delta-DV01 hedge and premium cost.

If rates rise 50 bps and futures fall 3.75 points at expiration, compute the portfolio loss, put payoff, and net hedged P&L using a whole-number hedge.

If rates instead fall 50 bps and the put expires worthless, compute net P&L.







NoteSolution





Portfolio DV01 is
\[DV01_P=\$12{,}000{,}000(7.50)(0.0001)=\boxed{\$9,000}.\]
The portfolio is equivalent to
\[N_{fut-eq}=\frac{9,000}{75}=\boxed{120\text{ futures contracts}}.\]
Because each put supplies only 0.45 short futures equivalent initially,
\[N_p=\frac{9,000}{0.45(75)}=266.67,\]
so use 267 puts. Premium cost is
\[267(1.10)(\$1,000)=\boxed{\$293,700}.\]
For a 50 bp rate rise, the duration loss is
\[-\$9,000(50)=-\$450,000.\]
The expiration futures price is \(112-3.75=108.25\). Each put pays \(111-108.25=2.75\) points, so total payoff is
\[267(2.75)(\$1,000)=\$734,250.\]
Net hedged P&L is
\[-450,000+734,250-293,700=\boxed{-\$9,450}.\]
If rates fall 50 bps, the mapped portfolio gain is \(\$450,000\). With no put payoff,
\[\text{net P\&L}=450,000-293,700=\boxed{\$156,300}.\]
The hedge is delta-neutral only for a small move when initiated. By expiration the put’s nonlinear payoff can create gains or losses different from a futures hedge, and the premium is paid in either scenario.

title: Assignment 2
text:
1.2 Question 2
A portfolio manager asks why Lecture 7 spends time modeling the short rate if today’s yield curve is already observable.
Answer the following:

Explain the difference between a yield curve and a short-rate model.

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis

1 Inputs and Assumptions
All values are illustrative, market-like inputs, not current quotes. The portfolio is intentionally small enough to audit by hand. Prices are near par; annual carry is approximated by spread times market value; spread duration is treated as constant; Treasury and spread P&L use first-order duration; PDs are physical one-year probabilities; defaults and mark-to-market spread changes are reported separately to avoid double counting.

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis
text:
2 Treasury and Spread Decomposition
For small changes,
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-D_T\Delta y_T-D_s\Delta s.
\]
Treasury duration measures exposure to the benchmark curve. Spread duration measures exposure to the bond’s compensation over that curve. DTS rewrites spread risk for a proportional spread shock:
\[
\text{DTS}=D_s s,
\qquad
\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx-\text{DTS}\frac{\Delta s}{s}.
\]


Code
portfolio_value = bonds["Market value ($mm)"].sum() * 1_000_000
treasury_dv01 = bonds["Treasury DV01 ($/bp)"].sum()
spread_dv01 = bonds["Spread DV01 ($/bp)"].sum()
portfolio_dts = bonds["Contribution to DTS"].sum()

pd.Series({
    "Portfolio value ($)": portfolio_value,
    "Treasury DV01 ($/bp)": treasury_dv01,
    "Spread DV01 ($/bp)": spread_dv01,
    "Portfolio DTS": portfolio_dts,
}).round(4)


Portfolio value ($)     3.5000e+07
Treasury DV01 ($/bp)    1.8020e+04
Spread DV01 ($/bp)      1.6440e+04
Portfolio DTS           7.5600e-02
dtype: float64


Equal market values do not imply equal credit risk. Wider-spread bonds can contribute disproportionately to DTS even when their spread duration is shorter.

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis
text:
3 Carry Versus Widening Breakeven
Approximate annual spread carry is \(MV\times s\). The spread widening that consumes one year of spread carry is
\[
\Delta s_{BE}\approx\frac{s}{D_s}.
\]
This is a mark-to-market breakeven, not a total-return forecast. It ignores rolldown, Treasury carry, default, taxes, and financing.

bonds["Annual spread carry ($)"] = (
    bonds["Market value ($mm)"] * 1_000_000 * bonds["Spread (bp)"] / 10_000
)
bonds["Widening breakeven (bp)"] = bonds["Spread (bp)"] / bonds["Spread duration"]

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis
text:
4 Expected Loss and Liquidity Reserve
Expected credit loss is
\[
EL=PD\times LGD\times EAD,
\qquad LGD=1-\text{Recovery Rate}.
\]
Spread is not expected loss. It may also compensate for systematic credit risk, uncertainty, liquidity, taxes, and supply-demand effects.

bonds["Expected loss ($)"] = (
    bonds["Market value ($mm)"] * 1_000_000 * bonds["One-year PD"] * bonds["LGD"]

bonds["Liquidity reserve ($)"] = (
    bonds["Market value ($mm)"] * 1_000_000 * bonds["Liquidity reserve (bp/year)"] / 10_000
)
bonds["Carry after EL and liquidity ($)"] = (
    bonds["Annual spread carry ($)"]
    - bonds["Expected loss ($)"]

5 Mild and Severe Scenarios
The scenarios distinguish a benchmark-rate shock from issuer spread shocks. Expected loss is shown as a separate one-year planning measure rather than added to scenario P&L.

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis
text:
6 Why the Risks Differ

Rate risk is exposure to the benchmark Treasury curve and can often be hedged with Treasury futures or swaps.
Spread risk is mark-to-market exposure to changing required compensation for credit and liquidity risk.
Default risk is a discrete credit event with uncertain recovery; PD and LGD describe expected loss, not daily spread volatility.
Liquidity risk is the cost or inability to trade near an observed price, often worst when spreads are already widening.

title: Practical Demo: Corporate-Bond Spread Risk and Scenario Analysis
text:
8 Financial Interpretation
A wide spread is not automatically attractive. The analyst should ask how much of the spread may be consumed by expected loss and liquidity, how much widening erases carry, and whether falling Treasury yields are likely to offset spread losses in stress. DTS is useful for proportional spread shocks; DV01 is useful for basis-point shocks; neither replaces explicit default and liquidity analysis.

title: Practical Demo: Callable-Bond Valuation, OAS, and Effective Risk
text:
2 Build a Recombining Short-Rate Tree
At time \(t\), node \(j\) has short rate
\[
r_{t,j}=m_t\exp\left[(2j-t)\sigma\right],
\]
where \(m_t\) is the median-rate path and \(\sigma\) controls annual volatility. Moving up increases \(j\) by one; moving down leaves \(j\) unchanged. Because the same number of up moves leads to the same node, the tree recombines.


Code
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

face = 100.0
coupon_rate = 0.0525
coupon = face * coupon_rate
maturity = 7
median_rates = np.array([0.0420, 0.0410, 0.0400, 0.0390, 0.0380, 0.0375, 0.0370])
rate_volatility = 0.18
up_probability = 0.50

call_schedule = {3: 101.50, 4: 101.00, 5: 100.50, 6: 100.00}

def build_rate_tree(medians, volatility, parallel_shift=0.0):
    """Return a recombining lognormal short-rate tree."""
    tree = []
    for t, median in enumerate(medians):
        nodes = np.array([
            median * np.exp((2 * j - t) * volatility) + parallel_shift
            for j in range(t + 1)
        ])
        if np.any(nodes <= -1.0):
            raise ValueError("A shocked node rate is below -100%.")
        tree.append(nodes)
    return tree

rate_tree = build_rate_tree(median_rates, rate_volatility)
rate_table = pd.DataFrame({
    f"Year {t}": pd.Series(100 * nodes)
    for t, nodes in enumerate(rate_tree)
}).round(3)
rate_table.index.name = "Node (number of up moves)"

title: Practical Demo: Callable-Bond Valuation, OAS, and Effective Risk
section: 3 Price the Option-Free and Callable Bonds
text:
3 Price the Option-Free and Callable Bonds
Values are measured immediately after any coupon at a node. The one-period holding value is
\[
V_{t,j}^{\text{hold}}
=
\frac{C+pV_{t+1,j+1}+(1-p)V_{t+1,j}}
{1+r_{t,j}+s}.
\]
For the option-free bond, this holding value is retained. At an eligible call date, the callable bond applies the issuer’s minimum rule:
\[
V_{t,j}^{\text{callable}}
=
\min\left\{V_{t,j}^{\text{hold}},\text{Call Price}_t\right\}.
\]


Code
def price_bond(rate_tree, spread=0.0, callable_bond=False, return_tree=False):
    """Price the bond by backward induction; node values are ex-coupon."""
    values = np.full(maturity + 1, face, dtype=float)
    value_tree = [None] * (maturity + 1)
    value_tree[maturity] = values.copy()

    for t in range(maturity - 1, -1, -1):
        expected_next = (
            (1 - up_probability) * values[:-1]
            + up_probability * values[1:]
        )
        hold_value = (coupon + expected_next) / (1 + rate_tree[t] + spread)
        if callable_bond and t in call_schedule:
            values = np.minimum(hold_value, call_schedule[t])
        else:
            values = hold_value
        value_tree[t] = values.copy()

    if return_tree:
        return float(values[0]), value_tree
    return float(values[0])

benchmark_straight_price = price_bond(rate_tree, spread=0.0)
benchmark_callable_price = price_bond(rate_tree, spread=0.0, callable_bond=True)
benchmark_option_cost = benchmark_straight_price - benchmark_callable_price

pd.Series({
    "Option-free value": benchmark_straight_price,
    "Callable value": benchmark_callable_price,
    "Embedded call value": benchmark_option_cost,
}).round(4)


Option-free value      107.0091
Callable value         103.3419
Embedded call value      3.6672
dtype: float64


The price decomposition is
\[
V_{\text{callable}}
=V_{\text{option-free}}-V_{\text{call option}}.
\]
The option cost is positive because the issuer owns the call. It is largest when low-rate paths make refinancing valuable.

title: Practical Demo: Callable-Bond Valuation, OAS, and Effective Risk
text:
4 Illustrate and Solve for OAS
To make the exercise reproducible, suppose the callable bond trades at the model value generated by an 85-basis-point spread. We then hide that spread and recover it from the price. In practice, the price would come from the market.


Code
illustrative_true_oas = 0.0085
market_price = price_bond(
    rate_tree,
    spread=illustrative_true_oas,
    callable_bond=True,
)

def solve_spread(target_price, callable_bond, lower=-0.02, upper=0.10, tolerance=1e-12):
    """Solve a constant spread with robust bisection."""
    price_lower = price_bond(rate_tree, lower, callable_bond)
    price_upper = price_bond(rate_tree, upper, callable_bond)
    if not (price_lower >= target_price >= price_upper):
        raise ValueError("Target price is not bracketed by the spread interval.")

    for _ in range(200):
        midpoint = 0.5 * (lower + upper)
        midpoint_price = price_bond(rate_tree, midpoint, callable_bond)
        if abs(midpoint_price - target_price) < tolerance:
            return midpoint
        if midpoint_price > target_price:
            lower = midpoint
        else:
            upper = midpoint
    return 0.5 * (lower + upper)

solved_oas = solve_spread(market_price, callable_bond=True)
static_spread = solve_spread(market_price, callable_bond=False)
option_cost_spread = static_spread - solved_oas
reprice = price_bond(rate_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond=True)

pd.Series({
    "Illustrative market price": market_price,
    "Solved OAS (bp)": solved_oas * 10_000,
    "Static spread on promised cash flows (bp)": static_spread * 10_000,
    "Option cost in spread terms (bp)": option_cost_spread * 10_000,
    "Repriced callable value": reprice,
}).round(6)


Illustrative market price                    100.0700
Solved OAS (bp)                               85.0000
Static spread on promised cash flows (bp)    115.8285
Option cost in spread terms (bp)              30.8285
Repriced callable value                      100.0700
dtype: float64


OAS is the spread left after the tree has modeled the issuer’s exercise decision. The static spread is larger because it discounts promised maturity cash flows and does not recognize that favorable low-rate paths can be taken away through a call.
The option cost can also be expressed in price terms at the solved OAS:


Code
straight_at_oas = price_bond(rate_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond=False)
callable_at_oas = price_bond(rate_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond=True)
option_cost_at_oas = straight_at_oas - callable_at_oas

pd.Series({
    "Option-free value at OAS": straight_at_oas,
    "Callable value at OAS": callable_at_oas,
    "Call option cost in price points": option_cost_at_oas,
}).round(4)

Callable value at OAS               100.0700
Call option cost in price points      1.7903

title: Practical Demo: Callable-Bond Valuation, OAS, and Effective Risk
text:
5 Effective Duration and Effective Convexity
Modified duration is not sufficient because the call decision changes across rate paths. Hold OAS fixed, shift the entire benchmark tree by \(\pm\Delta y\), and fully reprice:
\[
D_{\text{eff}}
=\frac{P_- - P_+}{2P_0\Delta y},
\]
\[
C_{\text{eff}}
=\frac{P_-+P_+-2P_0}{P_0(\Delta y)^2}.
\]


Code
curve_shock = 0.0025  # 25 basis points

def effective_risk(callable_bond):
    base = price_bond(rate_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond)
    down_tree = build_rate_tree(median_rates, rate_volatility, -curve_shock)
    up_tree = build_rate_tree(median_rates, rate_volatility, curve_shock)
    price_down = price_bond(down_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond)
    price_up = price_bond(up_tree, solved_oas, callable_bond)
    duration = (price_down - price_up) / (2 * base * curve_shock)
    convexity = (price_down + price_up - 2 * base) / (base * curve_shock**2)
    return base, price_down, price_up, duration, convexity

straight_risk = effective_risk(False)
callable_risk = effective_risk(True)

risk_table = pd.DataFrame(
    [straight_risk, callable_risk],
    index=["Option-free bond", "Callable bond"],
    columns=["P0", "P(-25 bp)", "P(+25 bp)", "Effective duration", "Effective convexity"],
)

text:
7 Financial Interpretation
This workflow separates three ideas that a yield-to-maturity comparison mixes together:

The benchmark short-rate tree values state-contingent cash flows.
The minimum rule transfers low-rate upside from the investor to the issuer.
OAS measures the constant spread that remains after the call option has been modeled.

The outputs are model-dependent. A different benchmark curve, volatility, call behavior, or tree calibration can materially change the option value, OAS, effective duration, and effective convexity.

3 Step 1: Record the observed Treasury curve
The published Treasury series contains par yields at standard maturity nodes. We retain the 1-, 2-, 3-, 5-, 7-, and 10-year observations and linearly interpolate missing integer maturities. The interpolation is an estimated curve-construction choice, not an additional market quote. For transparent annual bootstrapping we treat each interpolated par yield as the coupon on an annual-pay par bond. A production Treasury curve would instead use security-level prices, semiannual coupons, actual day counts, accrued interest, and bills at the short end.


Code
def price_annual_coupon_bond(coupon_rate, maturity, discount_factors, face=100.0):
    """Price an annual-pay bond from discount factors at integer years.

    discount_factors[k - 1] must equal P(0, k).
    """
    coupon = face * coupon_rate
    cash_flows = np.full(maturity, coupon)
    cash_flows[-1] += face
    return float(np.sum(cash_flows * discount_factors[:maturity]))

text:
4 Step 2: Bootstrap today’s discount curve
For the one-year bond, the only cash flow is coupon plus principal, so its price immediately gives \(P(0,1)\). For each later bond, discount factors for earlier coupons are already known. The final discount factor is the only unknown:
\[
P(0,n)=\frac{100-\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}C_nP(0,i)}{100+C_n},
\qquad C_n=100c_n.
\]


Code
def bootstrap_discount_factors(maturities, coupon_rates, bond_prices, face=100.0):
    """Bootstrap annual discount factors from annual-pay coupon bonds.

    Inputs
    ------
    maturities : array-like of integers
        Consecutive maturities 1, 2, ..., N.
    coupon_rates : array-like
        Annual coupon rates in decimal form.
    bond_prices : array-like
        Observed clean prices per 100 of face value.

    Output
    ------
    NumPy array
        Discount factors P(0, 1), ..., P(0, N).
    """
    maturities = np.asarray(maturities, dtype=int)
    coupon_rates = np.asarray(coupon_rates, dtype=float)
    bond_prices = np.asarray(bond_prices, dtype=float)

    expected = np.arange(1, len(maturities) + 1)
    if not np.array_equal(maturities, expected):
        raise ValueError("Maturities must be consecutive integers starting at 1.")

    discount_factors = np.empty(len(maturities))

    for row, maturity in enumerate(maturities):
        coupon = face * coupon_rates[row]

        # Present value of coupons before the maturity date.
        earlier_coupon_pv = coupon * discount_factors[:row].sum()

        # Solve the bond-pricing equation for the one remaining unknown.
        discount_factors[row] = (
            bond_prices[row] - earlier_coupon_pv
        ) / (face + coupon)

    return discount_factors


bootstrapped_discounts = bootstrap_discount_factors(
    maturities,
    coupon_rates,
    clean_prices,
)
bootstrapped_zero_rates = -np.log(bootstrapped_discounts) / maturities

curve_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "maturity_years": maturities,
    "discount_factor": bootstrapped_discounts,
    "zero_rate_pct": 100 * bootstrapped_zero_rates,

text:
6 Step 4: Fit the Hull–White dynamics to option prices
The lecture’s calibration logic separates two jobs:

the function \(\theta(t)\) makes the model fit today’s entire curve; and
\(a\) and \(\sigma\) control future mean reversion and volatility.

In practice, \(a\) and \(\sigma\) are fitted to liquid caps, floors, or swaptions. To keep the code transparent, our artificial option market consists of European calls on zero-coupon bonds. Such option premiums are observable, and Hull–White has a short closed-form pricing formula for them.

6.1 Hull–White building blocks
For the one-factor model
\[dr_t=[\theta(t)-a r_t]dt+\sigma dW_t,\]
define
\[B(t,T)=\frac{1-e^{-a(T-t)}}{a}.\]
The volatility of a zero-coupon bond option expiring at \(S\) on a bond maturing at \(T\) is
\[\sigma_P=\sigma B(S,T)\sqrt{\frac{1-e^{-2aS}}{2a}}.\]


Code
def normal_cdf(x):
    """Standard normal cumulative probability; works for scalars."""
    return 0.5 * (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0)))


def hw_B(start, end, mean_reversion):
    """Return the Hull–White B(start, end) loading."""
    return (1.0 - np.exp(-mean_reversion * (end - start))) / mean_reversion


def zero_bond_call_price(expiry, bond_maturity, strike,
                         mean_reversion, volatility, face=100.0):
    """Price a European call on a zero-coupon bond under Hull–White.

    The option expires at `expiry`. Its underlying pays `face` at
    `bond_maturity`. The strike is paid at expiry per `face` of principal.
    """
    p_0_s = float(discount_0(expiry))
    p_0_t = float(discount_0(bond_maturity))

    bond_vol = (
        volatility
        * hw_B(expiry, bond_maturity, mean_reversion)
        * math.sqrt((1.0 - math.exp(-2.0 * mean_reversion * expiry))
                    / (2.0 * mean_reversion))
    )

    # Work with values per $1 face, then multiply by face at the end.
    strike_per_dollar = strike / face
    h = (
        math.log(p_0_t / (strike_per_dollar * p_0_s)) / bond_vol
        + 0.5 * bond_vol
    )
    call_per_dollar = (
        p_0_t * normal_cdf(h)
        - strike_per_dollar * p_0_s * normal_cdf(h - bond_vol)
    )
    return face * call_per_dollar




6.2 Create a synthetic option quote snapshot
We create at-the-money-forward calls with expiries from six months to five years. The hidden values \(a=0.18\) and \(\sigma=1.20\%\) are used only to generate the market premiums. A small alternating bid/ask-like perturbation prevents a mechanically perfect parameter recovery.

6.3 Calibrate \(a\) and \(\sigma\) with a simple grid search
The objective is the root-mean-square pricing error across the option quotes. A grid search is slower than a numerical optimizer, but students can see exactly what is tried and it needs no extra package.

def option_rmse(mean_reversion, volatility):
    """Return RMSE between Hull–White and observed option prices."""
    model_prices = np.array([
        zero_bond_call_price(expiry, maturity, strike,
                             mean_reversion, volatility)
        for expiry, maturity, strike in zip(
            option_expiries, underlying_maturities, option_strikes
        )
    ])
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((model_prices - observed_option_prices) ** 2)))

    [option_rmse(a, sigma) for sigma in sigma_grid]
    for a in a_grid
])

calibrated_sigma = sigma_grid[best_col]

section: 7 Step 5: Fit the time-dependent drift to today’s curve
text:
7 Step 5: Fit the time-dependent drift to today’s curve
Once \(a\) and \(\sigma\) are known, the drift function that fits the observed initial curve is
\[
\theta(t)=\frac{\partial f(0,t)}{\partial t}
+a f(0,t)+\frac{\sigma^2}{2a}\left(1-e^{-2at}\right).
\]
This is the lecture’s key calibration point: \(\theta(t)\) is a function, not one number. It supplies enough flexibility to match all maturities of today’s curve.


Code
def theta(time, mean_reversion, volatility, step=1e-3):
    """Return the Hull–White drift theta(t) fitted to today's curve."""
    time = np.asarray(time, dtype=float)
    left = np.maximum(time - step, 0.0)
    right = time + step

    # Numerical derivative of today's instantaneous forward curve.
    forward_slope = (
        forward_rate_0(right) - forward_rate_0(left)
    ) / (right - left)

    return (
        forward_slope
        + mean_reversion * forward_rate_0(time)
        + volatility**2 / (2.0 * mean_reversion)
          * (1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 * mean_reversion * time))
    )


theta_times = np.linspace(0.05, 10.0, 400)
theta_values = theta(theta_times, calibrated_a, calibrated_sigma)

plt.plot(theta_times, 100 * theta_values, color=BLUE)
plt.xlabel("Time (years)")
plt.ylabel("$\theta(t)$ (% per year²)")
plt.title("Time-dependent drift required by today's market curve")
plt.show()









The sharp changes are a consequence of using simple piecewise-linear interpolation. That is instructive: curve construction and smoothing matter in real calibration.

7.1 Verify that Hull–White reproduces today’s discount curve
For future-date pricing, Hull–White gives the zero-coupon bond price
\[
P(t,T)=A(t,T)e^{-B(t,T)r_t},
\]
where
\[
A(t,T)=\frac{P(0,T)}{P(0,t)}
\exp\left[B(t,T)f(0,t)
-\frac{\sigma^2}{4a}(1-e^{-2at})B(t,T)^2\right].
\]
At \(t=0\), using \(r_0=f(0,0)\) makes the exponential terms cancel, leaving exactly \(P(0,T)\). This is the no-arbitrage fit.


Code
def hw_discount_factor(valuation_time, maturity, short_rate,
                       mean_reversion, volatility):
    """Return the Hull–White state-dependent discount factor P(t,T).

    Inputs
    ------
    valuation_time : float
        Future valuation date t, in years from today.
    maturity : number or array
        Payment date(s) T, with T > t.
    short_rate : float
        Short rate r_t observed or simulated at the valuation date.
    mean_reversion, volatility : float
        Calibrated Hull–White parameters a and sigma.
    """
    maturity = np.asarray(maturity, dtype=float)
    b_value = hw_B(valuation_time, maturity, mean_reversion)

    variance_adjustment = (
        volatility**2
        / (4.0 * mean_reversion)
        * (1.0 - np.exp(-2.0 * mean_reversion * valuation_time))
        * b_value**2
    )

    a_value = (
        discount_0(maturity) / discount_0(valuation_time)
        * np.exp(
            b_value * forward_rate_0(valuation_time)
            - variance_adjustment
        )
    )
    return a_value * np.exp(-b_value * short_rate)


r_0 = float(forward_rate_0(0.0))
hw_discounts_today = hw_discount_factor(
    0.0, maturities, r_0, calibrated_a, calibrated_sigma
)

8 Step 6: Generate future yield curves
Move to year 2. In a one-factor Hull–White model, the short rate \(r_2\) is the single state variable. Once a state is specified, hw_discount_factor() produces \(P(2,T)\) for every \(T>2\), and therefore the entire future zero curve:
\[y(2,T)=-\frac{\log P(2,T)}{T-2}.\]
We show three possible states around the model’s central short-rate level. They are scenarios, not point forecasts.

section: 9 Step 7: Use a future curve to price a bond
text:
9 Step 7: Use a future curve to price a bond
Consider the original ten-year 4.10% coupon bond at year 2, immediately after its year-2 coupon has been paid. Eight coupons and the principal remain. Its value in each state is simply the discounted value of those remaining cash flows using \(P(2,T)\).


Code
def price_bond_at_time(valuation_time, payment_times, cash_flows,
                       short_rate, mean_reversion, volatility):
    """Price fixed cash flows at a future date using a Hull–White curve.

    Output is the value at `valuation_time`, not today's value.
    """
    payment_times = np.asarray(payment_times, dtype=float)
    cash_flows = np.asarray(cash_flows, dtype=float)

    if np.any(payment_times <= valuation_time):
        raise ValueError("Every payment must occur after the valuation time.")

    future_discounts = hw_discount_factor(
        valuation_time,
        payment_times,
        short_rate,
        mean_reversion,
        volatility,
    )
    return float(np.sum(cash_flows * future_discounts))


payment_times = np.arange(3.0, 11.0)
remaining_cash_flows = np.full(len(payment_times), 4.10)
remaining_cash_flows[-1] += 100.0

future_bond_values = []
for state_name, short_rate in short_rate_states.items():
    value = price_bond_at_time(
        future_time,
        payment_times,
        remaining_cash_flows,
        short_rate,
        calibrated_a,
        calibrated_sigma,
    )
    future_bond_values.append({
        "state": state_name,
        "short_rate_pct": 100 * short_rate,
        "bond_value_at_year_2": value,
    })

title: Demo: From Observed Treasury Yields to Hull–White Future Curves
text:
10 Step 8: Plain-bond consistency at time 0
Finally, verify the lecture’s important claim: once Hull–White is calibrated to the observed curve, it does not create a different time-0 price for a vanilla bond. Both methods discount the same fixed cash flows with the same \(P(0,T)\).


Code
vanilla_payment_times = np.arange(1.0, 11.0)
vanilla_cash_flows = np.full(10, 4.10)
vanilla_cash_flows[-1] += 100.0

# Method 1: discount directly with today's observed/bootstrapped curve.
direct_curve_price = float(np.sum(
    vanilla_cash_flows * discount_0(vanilla_payment_times)
))

# Method 2: use the calibrated Hull–White zero-coupon formula at t = 0.
hw_curve_price = float(np.sum(
    vanilla_cash_flows
    * hw_discount_factor(
        0.0,
        vanilla_payment_times,
        r_0,
        calibrated_a,
        calibrated_sigma,
    )
))

print(f"Direct observed-curve price: {direct_curve_price:.10f}")
print(f"Calibrated Hull–White price:  {hw_curve_price:.10f}")
print(f"Difference:                    {hw_curve_price - direct_curve_price:.12f}")


Direct observed-curve price: 96.2742663687
Calibrated Hull–White price:  96.2742663687
Difference:                    0.000000000000


The equality is structural, not a coincidence. At time 0, the calibrated model uses the market discount factors by construction. For a vanilla bond, the model adds no new pricing information. Its value is the ability to generate future curves and to value cash flows that depend on those future states.

title: Demo: From Observed Treasury Yields to Hull–White Future Curves
text:
12 Takeaways

Market bond prices can be converted into discount factors by bootstrapping.
Hull–White does not fit a whole curve using only two constants. The function \(\theta(t)\) fits today’s term structure; \(a\) and \(\sigma\) describe future dynamics.
Option prices provide information about those dynamics that vanilla bond prices do not.
At a future date, each one-factor Hull–White short-rate state produces a complete yield curve and a value for the remaining cash flows.
A vanilla bond has the same time-0 value under calibrated Hull–White and direct curve discounting. The model earns its keep when future rates affect valuation or cash flows.







NoteSimplifications



Real desks use multiple instrument types, day-count conventions, accrued interest, bid/ask spreads, smooth curve interpolation, and robust numerical optimizers. The demo deliberately removes those layers so the economic logic stays visible.

title: Practical Demo: Duration, Convexity, and Portfolio Repricing
section: 1 Full Cash-Flow Pricing and Risk Measures
text:
1 Full Cash-Flow Pricing and Risk Measures
For cash flow \(CF_k\) at semiannual period \(k\),
\[
P=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{CF_k}{(1+y/m)^k}.
\]
Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average payment time. Modified duration is \(D_{Mac}/(1+y/m)\), and
\[
DV01=P D_{mod}(0.0001).
\]


Code
def bond_metrics(face, coupon_rate, maturity, ytm, frequency=2):
    periods = int(round(maturity * frequency))
    times = np.arange(1, periods + 1) / frequency
    cash_flows = np.full(periods, face * coupon_rate / frequency)
    cash_flows[-1] += face
    period_yield = ytm / frequency
    pv = cash_flows / (1 + period_yield) ** np.arange(1, periods + 1)
    price = pv.sum()
    macaulay = np.sum(times * pv) / price
    modified = macaulay / (1 + period_yield)
    k = np.arange(1, periods + 1)
    convexity = np.sum(
        cash_flows * k * (k + 1)
        / (frequency**2 * (1 + period_yield) ** (k + 2))
    ) / price
    dv01 = price * modified * 0.0001
    return price, macaulay, modified, dv01, convexity

rows = []
for bond in bonds.itertuples(index=False):
    face = bond[1] * 1_000_000
    metrics = bond_metrics(face, bond[2], bond[3], bond[4], frequency)
    rows.append(metrics)

metrics = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Price ($)", "Macaulay duration",
                                      "Modified duration", "DV01/PVBP ($/bp)", "Convexity"])
bond_risk = pd.concat([bonds, metrics], axis=1)

4 Parallel and Nonparallel Scenarios
A single duration number is designed for a parallel shift. A curve twist must be applied bond by bond.

scenario_shocks = {
    "Parallel +50 bp": np.array([50, 50, 50]),
    "Bear steepener": np.array([10, 35, 75]),
    "Bull flattener": np.array([-15, -45, -90]),
}

scenario_rows = []
for name, shocks in scenario_shocks.items():
    exact_pnl = 0.0
    duration_pnl = 0.0
    duration_convexity_pnl = 0.0
    for i, bond in bond_risk.iterrows():
        shock = shocks[i] / 10_000
        shocked_price = bond_metrics(
            bond["Face value ($mm)"] * 1_000_000, bond["Coupon rate"],
            bond["Maturity (years)"], bond["Yield"] + shock, frequency
        )[0]
        exact_pnl += shocked_price - bond["Price ($)"]
        duration_pnl += bond["Price ($)"] * (-bond["Modified duration"] * shock)
        duration_convexity_pnl += bond["Price ($)"] * (
            -bond["Modified duration"] * shock + 0.5 * bond["Convexity"] * shock**2
        )
    scenario_rows.append([name, duration_pnl, duration_convexity_pnl, exact_pnl])

scenario_results = pd.DataFrame(
    scenario_rows,
    columns=["Scenario", "Duration P&L ($)", "Duration + convexity P&L ($)", "Exact P&L ($)"],
).set_index("Scenario")

title: Practical Demo: Duration, Convexity, and Portfolio Repricing
text:
6 Financial Interpretation
Duration is a local slope, convexity is a curvature correction, and exact cash-flow repricing is the benchmark. DV01 translates percentage sensitivity into dollars. Portfolio aggregation is reliable for a stated parallel shock, but nonparallel scenarios require maturity-specific or key-rate exposures.

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
1 Big Picture: Two Credit Questions
Credit-risky bonds expose investors to two related but different questions:

Spread exposure: If the market demands more or less compensation for credit risk, how much will the bond price move?
Default exposure: What is the probability of default, what is the expected recovery, and how do defaults interact across a portfolio?

The first question is about mark-to-market risk. A corporate bond can lose value even if it never defaults because its credit spread widens. The second question is about credit events and losses. Both matter for portfolio construction.
For a plain corporate bond, a simple yield decomposition is:
\[
y_{\text{corp}} \approx y_{\text{Treasury}} + s,
\]
where \(s\) is the credit spread. A price change can then come from a change in Treasury yields, a change in credit spreads, or both.






TipCore Intuition



Treasury duration tells us how much the bond reacts to risk-free rates. Spread duration and DTS tell us how much the bond reacts to the market’s compensation for credit risk. Credit risk models go one level deeper and ask where that compensation should come from.










Figure 1: Corporate bond risk combines Treasury-rate exposure, spread exposure, and default exposure
crumbs: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
2 Measuring Changes in Credit Spreads
The credit spread of a risky bond is the difference between the yield on the risky bond and the yield on a comparable Treasury security:
\[
s_i = y_i - y_{\text{Treasury}}.
\]
There are two common ways to measure a spread change.
The absolute spread change is:
\[
\Delta s_i.
\]
The relative spread change is:
\[
\frac{\Delta s_i}{s_i}.
\]
The difference matters because a 25-basis-point widening does not mean the same thing for every bond.






NoteExample 1: Absolute Versus Relative Spread Changes



Suppose Bond A has a spread of 50 bps and Bond B has a spread of 500 bps.
If both spreads widen by 25 bps, the absolute change is the same:
\[
\Delta s_A = \Delta s_B = 25 \text{ bps}.
\]
But the relative changes are very different:
\[
\frac{25}{50}=50\%,
\qquad
\frac{25}{500}=5\%.
\]
For Bond A, the market has increased required credit compensation by half. For Bond B, the same 25 bps is a much smaller proportional shock.


If credit spread changes tend to be proportional to the starting spread level, then high-spread bonds should usually experience larger basis-point moves than tight-spread bonds. Empirical evidence supports this proportional view for corporate bonds. That is why relative spread changes are central to DTS.








Figure 2: The same absolute spread move can be a very different relative spread shock
crumbs: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
3 Measuring Credit Spread Sensitivity

Spread Duration
Spread duration measures the approximate percentage price change for a 100-basis-point parallel change in credit spreads, holding Treasury rates constant.
The approximate spread duration is:
\[
D_{\text{spread}}
=
\frac{P_- - P_+}{2P_0\Delta s},
\]
where:

\(P_0\) is the initial price;
\(P_-\) is the price after the spread decreases by \(\Delta s\);
\(P_+\) is the price after the spread increases by \(\Delta s\).

For small spread moves:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_{\text{spread}}}{P}
\approx
-D_{\text{spread}}\Delta s.
\]
The negative sign reflects the usual price-spread relationship. If spreads widen, prices fall.






NoteExample 2: Spread Duration Price Impact



Suppose a corporate bond has spread duration of 6.5. Its spread widens by 40 bps, or 0.0040.
The approximate percentage price change is:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}
\approx
-6.5(0.0040)
=
-0.026
=
-2.6\%.
\]
If the bond was priced at 98, the approximate price decline is:
\[
98 \times 2.6\% = 2.548
\]
points, so the new price is roughly 95.45.


Spread duration is useful, but it implicitly uses absolute spread changes. That is a limitation if high-spread bonds tend to have larger basis-point spread moves.


Duration Times Spread (DTS)
Duration times spread (DTS) is:
\[
\text{DTS} = D_{\text{spread}} \times s.
\]
If \(s\) is expressed in decimal form, DTS is also a decimal. A bond with spread duration 4 and spread 90 bps has:
\[
\text{DTS} = 4 \times 0.0090 = 0.036 = 3.6\%.
\]
The logic comes from rewriting the spread-price relation. Start with:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_{\text{spread}}}{P}
\approx
-D_{\text{spread}}\Delta s.
\]
Multiply and divide by \(s\):
\[
\frac{\Delta P_{\text{spread}}}{P}
\approx
-(D_{\text{spread}}s)\frac{\Delta s}{s}.
\]
The first term is DTS, and the second term is the relative spread change:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_{\text{spread}}}{P}
\approx
-\text{DTS}\times \frac{\Delta s}{s}.
\]






TipDTS Is Intuition



Spread duration asks: “What happens if every bond’s spread moves by the same number of basis points?”
DTS asks: “What happens if every bond’s spread moves by the same percentage of its starting spread?”
The second question often fits corporate spread behavior better because distressed or high-yield bonds usually have wider and more volatile spreads.








NoteExample 3: DTS and Relative Spread Shocks



Bond A has spread duration 7 and spread 100 bps, or 0.0100:
\[
\text{DTS}_A = 7(0.0100)=0.0700.
\]
Bond B has spread duration 3.5 and spread 400 bps, or 0.0400:
\[
\text{DTS}_B = 3.5(0.0400)=0.1400.
\]
If spreads widen by 20% relative to their starting levels, then:
\[
\frac{\Delta s}{s}=0.20.
\]
For Bond A:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_A}{P_A}
\approx
-0.0700(0.20)
=
-0.0140.
\]
So Bond A loses approximately 1.40%.
For Bond B:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_B}{P_B}
\approx
-0.1400(0.20)
=
-0.0280.
\]
So Bond B loses approximately 2.80%.
Bond B has shorter spread duration, but it has more credit spread risk because its starting spread is much wider.


For a portfolio, contribution to DTS is:
\[
\text{Contribution to DTS}_i
= w_i D_{\text{spread},i}s_i.
\]
This identifies where credit spread risk actually sits in the portfolio.






NoteExample 4: Portfolio DTS



Suppose a portfolio has three sectors.

Weight
Spread duration
Spread
DTS

A-rated industrials

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
4 Empirical Duration for Corporate Bonds
Corporate bond price performance is driven by more than one risk factor. The main exposures are:

Treasury-rate risk;
credit spread risk;
equity-like risk, especially for lower-rated issuers.

The relative importance of these risks depends on credit quality. For high-quality investment-grade bonds, the promised cash flows are more likely to be paid, so Treasury-rate risk is often the dominant driver of day-to-day price changes. If the 10-year Treasury yield rises, the price of a long-maturity A-rated corporate bond will usually fall in a way that looks similar to a Treasury bond with comparable duration.
For high-yield bonds, the story is different. The lower the issuer’s credit quality, the more investors focus on default probability, recovery value, refinancing risk, and the issuer’s business outlook. These risks are closer to equity risk than to pure interest-rate risk. This is why lower-rated high-yield bonds are often described as equity-like.
This distinction matters because the standard modified duration formula treats the bond as if its price response is mainly a discount-rate effect. That can be misleading for high-yield bonds. A high-yield bond may have an analytical duration of 5, but if its spread tightens when Treasury yields rise, or if its price is mainly driven by default and recovery expectations, its observed Treasury-rate sensitivity may be much lower.
Portfolio managers usually deal with this problem in one of two ways:

use a rule of thumb to reduce analytical duration for lower-rated bonds;
estimate empirical duration from historical price changes and Treasury yield changes.

For example, a manager might reduce a high-yield bond’s analytical duration by 75%. If the analytical duration is 5, the adjusted duration would be:
\[
5 \times 0.25 = 1.25.
\]
That adjustment is crude, but the intuition is right: lower-rated bonds often behave less like Treasuries and more like credit-risk assets.

Analytical Duration Versus Empirical Duration
Analytical duration is computed from the bond’s promised cash flows, price, yield, and maturity. It answers a mechanical repricing question: how would the price change if the discount yield changed while the cash flows remained promised?
Empirical duration is estimated from observed market behavior, commonly with a regression:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_t}{P_t}
=
\alpha - D_{\text{emp}}\Delta y_t + \epsilon_t.
\]
The estimated slope gives an empirical measure of how the bond actually moved when Treasury yields changed.
For an investment-grade bond, the regression line is usually steeper because price changes are more sensitive to Treasury yield changes. For a high-yield bond, the regression line is often flatter because spread and equity-like credit effects absorb more of the price movement.








Figure 4: Stylized empirical duration regressions: investment-grade bonds usually have steeper Treasury-rate sensitivity than high-yield bonds











TipCore Intuition



Analytical duration treats the bond like a promised-cash-flow instrument. Empirical duration recognizes that corporate bond spreads may move at the same time Treasury yields move. For risky bonds, the spread response can offset or amplify the Treasury-rate effect.




Theoretical Difference Between Analytical Duration and Empirical Duration
A simple two-factor approximation is:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}
\approx
-D\Delta y - D s \frac{\Delta s}{s},
\]
where \(D\) is modified duration, \(\Delta y\) is the Treasury yield change, \(s\) is the starting spread, and \(\Delta s/s\) is the relative spread change.
The first term,
\[
-D\Delta y,
\]
is the usual Treasury-rate duration effect. If Treasury yields rise, the bond price falls.
The second term,
\[
-D s \frac{\Delta s}{s},
\]
is the credit spread effect written in DTS form. Since \(\text{DTS}=Ds\), the spread-price effect can also be written as:
\[
-\text{DTS}\times \frac{\Delta s}{s}.
\]
So the two-factor approximation says that a corporate bond’s price changes because of both Treasury-rate changes and credit-spread changes.
To connect this to empirical duration, divide both sides by \(\Delta y\):
\[
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta y}
\approx
-D
-
Ds
\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}.
\]
Now factor out \(-D\):
\[
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta y}
\approx
-D
\left[
1
+
s
\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}
\right].
\]
The key object is:
\[
\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}.
\]
This measures how relative credit spread changes tend to move when Treasury yields change. Since that relationship is not known analytically, we estimate it empirically. The regression-style approximation is:
\[
\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}
\approx
\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}.
\]
This comes from the slope coefficient in a regression of relative spread changes on Treasury yield changes:
\[
\beta
=
\frac{\operatorname{cov}(\Delta y,\Delta s/s)}
{\operatorname{var}(\Delta y)}.
\]
Using
\[
\operatorname{cov}(\Delta y,\Delta s/s)
=
\rho_{y,s}\sigma_y\sigma_s
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{var}(\Delta y)=\sigma_y^2,
\]
we get:
\[
\beta
=
\frac{\rho_{y,s}\sigma_y\sigma_s}{\sigma_y^2}
=
\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}.
\]
Substituting this empirical relationship into the duration expression gives:
\[
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta y}
\approx
-D
\left[
1 + s\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}
\right],
\]
where:

\(\rho_{y,s}\) is the correlation between Treasury yield changes and relative spread changes;
\(\sigma_s\) is the volatility of relative spread changes;
\(\sigma_y\) is the volatility of Treasury yield changes.

The bracketed term is the duration adjustment.
If Treasury yields rise when credit spreads tighten, then \(\rho_{y,s}\) is negative. The bracketed term is less than 1, so empirical duration is lower than analytical duration. Intuitively, the Treasury-rate loss is partly offset by a gain from spread tightening.
If Treasury yields rise when credit spreads widen, then \(\rho_{y,s}\) is positive. The bracketed term is greater than 1, so empirical duration is higher than analytical duration. In that case, the Treasury-rate loss and spread-widening loss reinforce each other.






NoteExample 5: Analytical Duration versus Empirical Duration



Suppose a corporate bond has:

analytical duration \(D=6.0\);
starting credit spread \(s=3.00\%=0.0300\);
correlation between Treasury yield changes and relative spread changes \(\rho_{y,s}=-0.50\);
volatility of relative spread changes \(\sigma_s=2.00\%=0.0200\);
volatility of Treasury yield changes \(\sigma_y=0.20\%=0.0020\).

The duration adjustment is:
\[
1 + s\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}
=
1 + (0.0300)(-0.50)\frac{0.0200}{0.0020}.
\]
Since
\[
\frac{0.0200}{0.0020}=10,
\]
the adjustment becomes:
\[
1 + (0.0300)(-0.50)(10)
=
1 - 0.1500
=
0.8500.
\]
So the empirical duration estimate is:
\[
D_{\text{emp}}
=
6.0(0.8500)
=
5.10.
\]
If Treasury yields rise by 50 bps, or 0.0050, the predicted relative price change is:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}
\approx
-5.10(0.0050)
=
-0.0255.
\]
So the bond price is expected to decline by about 2.55%, not the 3.00% decline implied by the analytical duration alone.








NoteExample 6: Why Empirical Duration Can Be Lower



Suppose a bond has analytical duration 6 and spread 3%. A 50 bps rise in Treasury yields would mechanically imply:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx -6(0.0050)=-3.0\%.
\]
But suppose the stronger economic environment also causes the bond’s spread to tighten by 30 bps:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_{\text{spread}}}{P}\approx -6(-0.0030)=+1.8\%.
\]
The combined price change is:
\[
-3.0\% + 1.8\% = -1.2\%.
\]
Relative to the 50 bps Treasury move, the observed duration is:
\[
\frac{1.2\%}{0.50\%}=2.4,
\]
not 6. The bond did not become short maturity. Its credit spread moved in the opposite direction and offset much of the rate effect.




Duration Multipliers
A duration multiplier adjusts analytical duration to approximate true Treasury-rate sensitivity:
\[
D_{\text{emp}} \approx M D_{\text{analytical}}.
\]
Empirical work often models the multiplier as a function of rating and spread:
\[
M = a + bs.
\]
Lower-rated and wider-spread bonds tend to have lower multipliers. In stressed or high-yield cases, the multiplier can be near zero or even negative if spread tightening during rate increases more than offsets the Treasury-rate price effect.






TipEstimating Duration Multipliers



Duration multipliers are usually estimated in two steps.
First, estimate empirical duration from bond price changes and Treasury yield changes:
\[
\frac{\Delta P_t}{P_t}
=
\alpha
-
D_{\text{emp}}\Delta y_t
+
\epsilon_t.
\]
Then compare empirical duration with analytical duration:
\[
M_i
=
\frac{D_{\text{emp},i}}{D_{\text{analytical},i}}.
\]
After estimating \(M_i\) for many bonds or rating/spread groups, researchers often regress the multiplier on a constant and the bond’s spread:
\[
M_i = a + bs_i + u_i.
\]
The intercept \(a\) is the baseline multiplier for that rating group. The slope \(b\) shows how the multiplier changes as spreads widen. Usually \(b<0\), meaning wider-spread bonds tend to have lower Treasury-rate sensitivity.








Figure 5: Estimating duration multipliers across many bonds













NoteExample 7: Using a Duration Multiplier



Suppose a portfolio manager holds $10 million of a B-rated bond. The bond has analytical duration of 5.0, but the estimated duration multiplier for bonds with its rating and spread is 0.25. The manager wants to estimate the bond’s response to a 75 bps increase in Treasury yields.
First, adjust the analytical duration:
\[
D_{\text{adjusted}} = 0.25(5.0)=1.25.
\]
Using analytical duration alone, the estimated price change would be:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}
\approx
-5.0(0.0075)
=-3.75\%.
\]
This implies a dollar loss of:
\[
10{,}000{,}000(0.0375)=\$375{,}000.
\]
Using the duration multiplier, the estimated Treasury-rate effect is instead:
\[
\frac{\Delta P}{P}
\approx
-1.25(0.0075)
=-0.9375\%.
\]
The corresponding dollar loss is:
\[
10{,}000{,}000(0.009375)=\$93{,}750.
\]
The multiplier reduces the estimated Treasury-rate exposure from $375,000 to $93,750. The difference reflects the historical tendency of the bond’s spread movement to offset part of its analytical rate sensitivity. This is the adjusted exposure the manager would use when sizing a Treasury hedge, before allowing for additional idiosyncratic credit movement.


The implication for portfolio management is important. If a manager uses analytical duration for high-yield bonds without adjustment, the portfolio’s reported rate exposure may be too high. Hedging based on that duration can create an unintended rate bet.






NoteExample 8: Portfolio Duration Misstatement



A portfolio manager targets duration of 5.5 and allocates 15% to high-yield bonds with analytical duration 5.0. The remaining 85% has duration 5.8.
Using analytical duration:
\[
0.85(5.8)+0.15(5.0)=5.68.
\]
This appears above the 5.5 target.
If the high-yield duration multiplier is 0.25, true high-yield duration is:
\[
0.25(5.0)=1.25.
\]
The true portfolio duration is:
\[
0.85(5.8)+0.15(1.25)=5.12.
\]
The portfolio is actually below the target. A hedge based on analytical duration would move the portfolio in the wrong direction.










Figure 6: Duration multipliers typically decline as credit quality weakens

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
5 Difficulties in Credit Risk Modeling
Credit risk is harder to model than interest-rate risk for several reasons.
First, default is a rare event. Treasury yields are observed every trading day. Defaults, especially for investment-grade issuers, occur infrequently. This means there is less data for estimating default probabilities and recoveries.
Second, issuers are heterogeneous. Companies differ by industry, leverage, size, asset quality, management, accounting choices, legal jurisdiction, and financing structure. Two firms with the same rating may have different risk profiles.
Third, defaults have many causes. A default may be driven by poor management, excess leverage, fraud, commodity prices, litigation, recession, high interest rates, or a liquidity shock. A model that works well in one default cycle may not work as well in another.
Fourth, recovery is uncertain. Even after default, the final loss depends on bankruptcy law, collateral, seniority, restructuring negotiations, and market conditions.






TipModeling Implication



Interest-rate modeling is usually about a liquid, frequently observed market variable. Credit modeling is about a rare event whose probability depends on balance sheets, market prices, legal rules, and macroeconomic states.
crumbs: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
6 Overview of Credit Risk Modeling
Credit risk models are used for three related tasks:

Estimating default probabilities.
Pricing credit-risky bonds and credit derivatives.
Measuring portfolio credit risk.

A default probability is the likelihood that a borrower defaults over a specified horizon. Models may produce a one-year default probability, a five-year default probability, or an entire term structure of default probabilities.
Pricing requires more than default probability. A model also needs:

recovery assumptions;
a risk-free term structure;
compensation for systematic credit risk, liquidity risk, and uncertainty about default timing.

Portfolio credit risk requires a dependence model. A portfolio of 100 bonds is not just 100 independent default probabilities. If defaults cluster in recessions, portfolio loss risk can be much larger than an independence assumption would imply.






NoteExample 9: Expected Loss Is Only a Starting Point



Suppose a one-year bond has:

probability of default \(PD=2\%\);
loss given default \(LGD=60\%\).

The expected credit loss is:
\[
EL = PD \times LGD = 2\% \times 60\% = 1.2\%.
\]
If the risk-free yield is 4%, a naive expected-loss spread might be about 120 bps. But market spreads also include risk premiums, liquidity premiums, taxes, and compensation for uncertainty. A 120 bps expected loss does not mean the fair market spread must equal 120 bps.

section: 7 Credit Ratings versus Credit Risk Models
text:
7 Credit Ratings versus Credit Risk Models
Credit ratings summarize an agency’s opinion of credit quality. They are useful, but they are not the same as model-implied default probabilities.








Feature
Credit ratings
Credit risk models




Scale
Discrete grades
Continuous probabilities


Update frequency
Infrequent
Can update daily or intraday


Horizon
Often broad short-term or long-term view
Can produce maturity-specific default probabilities


Inputs
Fundamental review and agency judgment
Market data, accounting data, macro variables, model assumptions


Strength
Stable, widely understood benchmark
Timely, granular, useful for pricing and risk


Weakness
Slow-moving and coarse
Model risk and calibration risk



Ratings still matter because many investors, mandates, indexes, and regulations use them. Models matter because market risk can change faster than ratings.






TipPractical View



Ratings are labels. Models are measurement systems. A good credit process usually compares both rather than treating either one as sufficient.

title: Lecture 10: Credit Spread Exposure and Credit Risk Modeling
text:
8 Structural Models
Structural models explain default using the firm’s balance sheet. The central idea is simple:

Default occurs when the value of the firm’s assets is too low relative to its debt obligations.

In these models, default is endogenous. It comes from the modeled value of the firm, leverage, volatility, and a default threshold.

Fundamentals of the Black-Scholes-Merton Model
The Black-Scholes-Merton (BSM) framework views corporate debt and equity through option-pricing logic.
Assume:

the firm has assets worth \(A(t)\);
it has one zero-coupon debt issue with face value \(K\) due at time \(T\);
equity holders decide at maturity whether to repay debt or default.

The key default rule is:
\[
\text{default at } T \quad \text{if} \quad A(T)<K.
\]
If assets are worth more than the promised debt payment, equity holders repay the debt and keep the residual firm value. If assets are worth less than the promised debt payment, equity holders walk away. Bondholders receive the firm assets, which are worth less than the promised amount.
This gives the model a direct default-probability interpretation:
\[
PD = \Pr[A(T)<K].
\]
The model assumes asset value follows a stochastic process, commonly a lognormal process. Therefore, default risk comes from the probability that the future asset-value distribution ends below the debt threshold \(K\).








Figure 7: In the basic BSM model, default occurs at maturity if asset value ends below the debt threshold





At maturity:
\[
E(T)=\max[A(T)-K,0].
\]
Equity is a call option on the firm’s assets with strike price \(K\).
Debt value at maturity can be written as:
\[
B(T)=A(T)-\max[A(T)-K,0].
\]
It can also be written as:
\[
B(T)=K-\max[K-A(T),0].
\]
This says risky debt is equivalent to a risk-free bond minus a put option on the firm’s assets. The put represents default risk.






NoteExample 10: BSM Payoffs at Maturity



Suppose debt face value is \(K=100\).



Asset value at maturity
Equity payoff
Debt payoff
