The protective put buys convexity. The covered call sells convexity. Neither is automatically superior; the correct choice depends on the manager’s objective, constraints, valuation view, and tolerance for tail outcomes.

title: Lecture 11: Interest-Rate Options
text:
14 A Complete Decision Framework
Before using an interest-rate option, ask five questions:

What is the underlying risk? A parallel rate move, a curve point, volatility, or an event date?
What payoff shape is desired? Lock, floor, cap, or premium income?
Which contract best matches the risk? Cash-bond option, futures option, cap, floor, or swaption?
How many contracts are needed? Use DV01, key-rate duration, beta, and option delta rather than notional value alone.
What can break the hedge? Basis, volatility, time decay, exercise, liquidity, margin, and model risk.









Figure 13: Choose the instrument from the desired payoff rather than from a market forecast alone

title: Lecture 11: Interest-Rate Options
text:
Check Your Understanding

A manager expects the 10-year yield to rise sharply. Should the manager buy a call or a put on 10-year Treasury futures? Explain both links in the chain.
A 110 put costs 0-32. What is its dollar premium? At what futures price does it break even at expiration, ignoring fees?
Why is the risk-neutral probability in a binomial tree not necessarily the market’s forecast probability?
A put hedge has delta \(-0.25\). Why might dividing portfolio DV01 only by futures DV01 materially understate the number of puts required initially?
Does a market-implied volatility prove that traders expect exactly that realized volatility? Why or why not?







NoteAnswers






Buy a put: rising yields usually lower Treasury prices, and a put benefits when the futures price falls.
\(0\text{-}32=32/64=0.5\) point, or \(\$500\). Break-even is \(110-0.5=109.5\), quoted as 109-32.
It enforces no-arbitrage pricing and a risk-free expected return; it is not estimated from real-world frequencies.
Each put initially supplies only 0.25 of one futures contract’s price sensitivity, so roughly four puts are needed for one futures-equivalent unit before other adjustments.
No. Implied volatility is a model-consistent price quote that also reflects risk premiums, supply and demand, liquidity, and model limitations.

title: Lecture 11: Interest-Rate Options
text:
Key Points

An option buyer has a right; an option writer has a contingent obligation.
Calls benefit from higher underlying prices, while puts benefit from lower underlying prices.
Futures create symmetric linear exposure; options create asymmetric exposure in exchange for a premium.
Exercising a futures call creates a long futures position at the strike; exercising a futures put creates a short futures position at the strike.
Treasury and SOFR futures options are important exchange-traded interest-rate options with standardized clearing and American-style exercise.
Intrinsic value is the value of immediate exercise. Time value is the premium above intrinsic value.
Long-option losses are limited to premium. Naked short-option profits are limited to premium while losses can be much larger.
Put-call parity links calls, puts, the underlying, and the present value of the strike through no-arbitrage.
Call value generally rises with the underlying price, time, and volatility and falls with the strike and interim coupon value.
Black-Scholes provides a transparent benchmark for European bond options, but its constant-volatility and lognormal assumptions are approximations.
A binomial model prices by backward induction and can incorporate early exercise.
Implied volatility is the model volatility consistent with an observed market price; it is not automatically a forecast of realized volatility.
Black’s model uses the futures price to value European options on bond futures.
Protective puts establish a floor while retaining upside, at the cost of premium.
Covered calls earn premium but cap gains and provide only limited downside cushion.
Effective hedges use DV01, delta, curve exposure, and basis relationships—not notional value alone.

title: Lecture 11: Interest-Rate Options
text:

Fabozzi, Bond Markets: Analysis and Strategies, chapters on interest-rate options.
CME Group, Fundamentals of Options on Futures.
CME Group, Trading SOFR Options.
CME Group, Primer on Margining Styles for Options.


Real-Market Data and Resources

OCC, Quarterly Report on Bank Trading and Derivatives Activities: See how interest-rate derivatives exposures are distributed across U.S. commercial banks.
Federal Reserve, Selected Interest Rates (H.15): Obtain the official underlying rate and Treasury-yield history needed to compare option-implied and subsequently realized rate movements.

title: Practical Demo: Constructing a Benchmark-Aware Bond Portfolio
text:
5 5. Construct a Constrained Active Portfolio
Let \(a=w-w_B\) be active weights and \(B\) the factor-exposure matrix. A compact factor-risk approximation is
\[TE^2 \approx (B'a)'\Sigma_F(B'a)+\sum_i a_i^2\sigma_{\epsilon,i}^2.\]
The objective balances predicted tracking error, turnover, transaction cost, and a modest preference for carry:
\[\min_w\; TE^2+\lambda_T\sum_i(w_i-w_i^{current})^2
+\lambda_C\sum_i c_i|w_i-w_i^{current}|-\lambda_Y w'y.\]
This is a teaching risk model. Production construction would use a validated factor covariance matrix, specific-risk forecasts, executable costs, lot sizes, and compliance-tested constraints.


Code
exposure_matrix = universe[factor_columns].to_numpy()
factor_vol = np.array([0.0070, 0.0080, 0.0090, 0.0060])
factor_correlation = np.array([
    [1.00, 0.82, 0.62, 0.05], [0.82, 1.00, 0.85, 0.08],
    [0.62, 0.85, 1.00, 0.10], [0.05, 0.08, 0.10, 1.00],
])
factor_covariance = np.outer(factor_vol, factor_vol) * factor_correlation
specific_vol = np.where(universe["Sector"].eq("Corporate"), 0.010, 0.003)
cost_rate = universe["Trading cost (bp)"].to_numpy() / 10_000
benchmark_duration = benchmark_weights @ universe["Duration"]

def tracking_variance(weights):
    active = weights - benchmark_weights
    active_factors = active @ exposure_matrix
    return active_factors @ factor_covariance @ active_factors + np.sum((active * specific_vol) ** 2)

def objective(weights):
    turnover_penalty = 0.002 * np.sum((weights - current_weights) ** 2)
    transaction_cost = 0.20 * np.sum(cost_rate * np.abs(weights - current_weights))
    carry_reward = 0.0015 * weights @ universe["Yield"]
    return tracking_variance(weights) + turnover_penalty + transaction_cost - carry_reward




Code
treasury_mask = universe["Sector"].eq("Treasury").to_numpy()
corporate_mask = universe["Sector"].eq("Corporate").to_numpy()
constraints = [
    {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: w.sum() - 1},
    {"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda w: w[treasury_mask].sum() - treasury_minimum},
    {"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda w: corporate_cap - w[corporate_mask].sum()},
    {"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda w: duration_tolerance -
     abs(w @ universe["Duration"].to_numpy() - benchmark_duration)},
]
solution = minimize(objective, current_weights, method="SLSQP",
                    bounds=[(0, position_cap)] * len(universe), constraints=constraints,
                    options={"ftol": 1e-12, "maxiter": 2_000})
assert solution.success, solution.message
optimized_weights = solution.x

    "Bull flattener": {"short": -20, "intermediate": -55, "long": -90, "spread": -10},

def scenario_return(weights, scenario):
    rate_shock = np.where(universe["Duration"].lt(3.5), scenario["short"],
                 np.where(universe["Duration"].lt(6.5), scenario["intermediate"], scenario["long"])) / 10_000
    spread_shock = np.where(universe["Sector"].eq("Corporate"), scenario["spread"],
                           np.where(universe["Sector"].eq("Agency"), scenario["spread"] * 0.25, 0)) / 10_000
    security_return = (-universe["Duration"].to_numpy() * rate_shock
                       - universe["Spread duration"].to_numpy() * spread_shock
                       + 0.5 * universe["Convexity"].to_numpy() * rate_shock**2)
    return weights @ security_return

           for scenario_name, shock in scenarios.items()}

title: Practical Demo: Vasicek Rate Scenarios and Long-Run Behavior
text:
The Vasicek model is
\[
dr_t=\kappa(\theta-r_t)dt+\sigma dW_t.
\]
This demo estimates its parameters from a dated monthly U.S. effective federal funds-rate history, simulates scenarios, checks long-run moments, and uses the fitted distribution for a one-year risk decision. The embedded observations are monthly averages for January 2023 through June 2025, recorded in percent and converted to decimals. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis, Effective Federal Funds Rate (FEDFUNDS). Parameters are constant; estimation error, regime shifts, jumps, and term premia are ignored. This short sample is pedagogical and should not be treated as a robust trading calibration.

title: Practical Demo: Vasicek Rate Scenarios and Long-Run Behavior
text:
2 Step 2: Estimate Vasicek parameters
The exact monthly transition can be written as an AR(1):
\[
r_{t+\Delta}=\alpha+\phi r_t+\varepsilon_{t+\Delta},\qquad
\phi=e^{-\kappa\Delta},\qquad \alpha=\theta(1-\phi).
\]
After OLS estimation,
\[
\widehat\kappa=-\frac{\log\widehat\phi}{\Delta},\qquad
\widehat\theta=\frac{\widehat\alpha}{1-\widehat\phi},\qquad
\widehat\sigma=s_\varepsilon
\sqrt{\frac{2\widehat\kappa}{1-\widehat\phi^2}}.
\]
Here \(\Delta=1/12\) year, \(\kappa\) is in \(1/\text{year}\), and \(\sigma\) is in decimal rate units per \(\sqrt{\text{year}}\).


Code
dt = 1 / 12
x = history.iloc[:-1].to_numpy()
y = history.iloc[1:].to_numpy()
design = np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x])
alpha_hat, phi_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(design, y, rcond=None)[0]
residuals = y - (alpha_hat + phi_hat * x)
residual_std = residuals.std(ddof=2)

if not 0 < phi_hat < 1:
    raise ValueError("This sample does not imply a stationary Vasicek fit.")

kappa = -np.log(phi_hat) / dt
theta = alpha_hat / (1 - phi_hat)
sigma = residual_std * np.sqrt(2 * kappa / (1 - phi_hat**2))
r0 = float(history.iloc[-1])

half_life = np.log(2) / kappa
long_run_std = sigma / np.sqrt(2 * kappa)

pd.Series({
    "Current rate": r0,
    "Estimated monthly persistence phi": phi_hat,
    "Mean-reversion speed kappa (1/year)": kappa,
    "Long-run mean theta": theta,
    "Volatility sigma (rate/sqrt(year))": sigma,
    "Mean-reversion half-life (years)": half_life,
    "Long-run standard deviation": long_run_std,
}).round(5)


Current rate                           0.0433
Estimated monthly persistence phi      0.9578
Mean-reversion speed kappa (1/year)    0.5173
Long-run mean theta                    0.0495
Volatility sigma (rate/sqrt(year))     0.0043
Mean-reversion half-life (years)       1.3399
Long-run standard deviation            0.0042
dtype: float64



\(\kappa\) controls how quickly shocks decay; the half-life is \(\ln(2)/\kappa\).
\(\theta\) is the long-run mean under the chosen probability measure.
\(\sigma\) controls the size of random innovations and the long-run dispersion.

title: Practical Demo: Vasicek Rate Scenarios and Long-Run Behavior
text:
3 Simulate Monthly Paths
The exact Vasicek transition is normal:
\[
r_{t+\Delta}=\theta+(r_t-\theta)e^{-\kappa\Delta}
+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1-e^{-2\kappa\Delta}}{2\kappa}}Z.
\]


Code
rng = np.random.default_rng(411)

def simulate_vasicek(initial_rate, years, paths, rng):
    steps = int(round(years / dt))
    output = np.empty((steps + 1, paths))
    output[0] = initial_rate
    persistence = np.exp(-kappa * dt)
    innovation_std = sigma * np.sqrt((1 - np.exp(-2 * kappa * dt)) / (2 * kappa))
    for t in range(steps):
        output[t + 1] = (
            theta + (output[t] - theta) * persistence
            + innovation_std * rng.standard_normal(paths)
        )
    return output

paths = simulate_vasicek(r0, years=5, paths=5_000, rng=rng)
time = np.arange(paths.shape[0]) * dt




Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.1))
for i in range(30):
    ax.plot(time, 100 * paths[:, i], alpha=0.28, linewidth=0.8)
ax.plot(time, 100 * paths.mean(axis=1), color="black", linewidth=2.2, label="Simulation mean")
ax.axhline(100 * theta, color="#F58518", linestyle="--", label="Long-run mean")
ax.set(xlabel="Years", ylabel="Short rate (%)", title="Illustrative Vasicek scenarios")
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax.legend()

Vasicek rates are normally distributed, so negative rates are possible. That can be useful in markets where negative policy rates are plausible, but it may be undesirable for other applications. A positivity-preserving model such as CIR changes this feature, at the cost of a different distribution and dynamics.

5 Use the fitted distribution in a funding decision
Suppose a treasury team wants a one-year planning range for a floating-rate funding cost tied to the overnight rate. Simulate 50,000 one-year endpoints and report the central 90% range and the probability that the rate exceeds 5%. This applies the fitted physical-measure model; it is not a risk-neutral bond price.

    r0, years=1.0, paths=50_000, rng=np.random.default_rng(414)
)[-1]

    "Median funding rate (%)": 100 * np.median(one_year_rates),

title: Practical Demo: Vasicek Rate Scenarios and Long-Run Behavior
text:
8 Financial Interpretation
Mean reversion makes the expected rate move toward \(\theta\), while volatility keeps future rates dispersed. \(\kappa\) determines how quickly today’s rate loses influence; \(\sigma\) determines scenario width. The model is a disciplined scenario generator, not a forecast guarantee. Calibration window, probability measure, structural breaks, and the normal model’s negative-rate tail all affect how its output should be used.

1 Market Inputs Versus Illustrative Inputs
The workflow resembles a daily risk-management task, but every number below is illustrative rather than live market data. A live hedge would use current positions, clean prices, accrued interest, key-rate durations, deliverable-basket data, conversion factors, CTD candidates, financing rates, and exchange contract specifications.
Simplifying assumptions:

changes are small enough for first-order DV01 approximations;
the selected CTD remains unchanged;
futures DV01 is constant over the scenario;
the Treasury move is parallel;
spread duration equals modified duration for the corporate positions;
yield betas summarize how each position historically responds to Treasury yields; and
transaction costs, margin cash flows, convexity, carry, and roll are ignored.

3 Frame the CTD and Conversion-Factor Problem
Treasury futures are linked to a delivery basket. The short chooses the eligible security to deliver, and the cheapest-to-deliver issue often determines the futures contract’s effective interest-rate sensitivity.
Suppose the current CTD candidate has the following illustrative inputs:



Input
Value




CTD clean price
101.75

7.35


Deliverable face amount
$100,000


Conversion factor
0.9275


Futures price
112-16 = 112.50



Ignoring accrued interest and delivery-option details,
\[
DV01_{CTD}
=D_{\text{mod,CTD}}P_{CTD}(0.0001),
\]
and
\[
DV01_{futures}\approx\frac{DV01_{CTD}}{CF}.
\]

4 Size and Round the Hedge
The portfolio is long bonds and loses when rates rise, so the hedge shorts Treasury futures. The exact contract count is
\[
N^*
=\frac{DV01_{portfolio}^{\text{Treasury}}}{DV01_{futures}}.
\]


Code
exact_contracts = treasury_dv01 / futures_dv01
rounded_contracts = int(np.rint(exact_contracts))
hedge_dv01 = rounded_contracts * futures_dv01
residual_treasury_dv01 = treasury_dv01 - hedge_dv01
hedge_ratio = hedge_dv01 / treasury_dv01

    "Rounded contracts to short": rounded_contracts,

title: Practical Demo: Hedging a Bond Portfolio with Treasury Futures
text:
5 Before-and-After Scenario P&L
Suppose Treasury yields rise by 35 basis points. Corporate spreads also widen by the amounts in the portfolio table. The first-order bond P&L is separated into Treasury and spread components:
\[
\Delta V_{portfolio}
\approx
-DV01^{\text{Treasury}}\Delta y_{Treasury}
-DV01^{\text{spread}}\Delta s.
\]
Because the hedge is short futures, its approximate gain when Treasury yields rise is
\[
\Delta V_{futures}
\approx
N\times DV01_{futures}\times\Delta y_{Treasury}.
\]


Code

    * portfolio["Spread shock in scenario (bp)"]
)
portfolio["Total unhedged P&L ($)"] = (
    portfolio["Treasury P&L ($)"] + portfolio["Spread P&L ($)"]
)

hedged_pnl = unhedged_pnl + futures_pnl
residual_rate_pnl = -residual_treasury_dv01 * treasury_shock_bp
spread_pnl = portfolio["Spread P&L ($)"].sum()

title: Practical Demo: Hedging a Bond Portfolio with Treasury Futures
text:
7 What Can Break the Hedge?

Basis risk: cash bonds and the futures contract may not move together.
Curve risk: one CTD-based DV01 cannot hedge every key-rate exposure.
Spread risk: Treasury futures do not directly hedge corporate credit spreads.
Yield-beta error: historical betas can change in stress periods.
CTD switching: a different deliverable bond can become cheapest to deliver.
Conversion-factor and delivery-option effects: the simple DV01 scaling is approximate.
Convexity: large yield moves make a first-order DV01 hedge less accurate.
Rounding, liquidity, margin, and roll: implementation affects realized results.

title: Practical Demo: Hedging with Options on Treasury Futures
text:
1 Inputs and Assumptions
All inputs are illustrative, market-like inputs, not live quotes. The option is treated as European for Black-model transparency; actual contract exercise and margin conventions must be checked. The bond portfolio is mapped to one Treasury futures contract with DV01; the CTD, conversion factor, basis, convexity, transaction costs, margin cash flows, and early exercise are held fixed or ignored.







Workflow stage
In this case

Futures, strike, quoted premium, expiry, and portfolio DV01


Estimated

Diagnosed
Quote-versus-model gap, intrinsic value, and time value


Used for
Choosing between a linear hedge and asymmetric protection





Code
import math
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

portfolio_value = 25_000_000
portfolio_dv01 = 18_000
futures_price = 112.00
strike = 111.00
futures_dv01 = 78.00
dollars_per_point = 1_000
time_to_expiry = 0.50
risk_free_rate = 0.042
volatility = 0.075

title: Practical Demo: Hedging with Options on Treasury Futures
text:
2 Treasury Option Quote Convention
Treasury futures and their options are quoted in price points and fractions. For a $100,000 face-value contract, one full point is $1,000 and 1/64 of a point is $15.625. A premium of 1-54 means
\[
1+\frac{54}{64}=1.84375\text{ points},
\]
or $1,843.75 per contract. Price points, dollars, and yield basis points are different units.


Code
quoted_points = 1 + 54 / 64
quoted_dollars = quoted_points * dollars_per_point
pd.Series({"Quoted premium (points)": quoted_points,
           "Quoted premium ($/contract)": quoted_dollars})


Quoted premium (points)           1.8438
Quoted premium ($/contract)    1843.7500

title: Practical Demo: Hedging with Options on Treasury Futures
section: 3 Intrinsic Value, Time Value, and Black’s Model
text:
3 Intrinsic Value, Time Value, and Black’s Model
For a futures put, intrinsic value is \(\max(K-F,0)\). Black’s European futures-put formula is
\[
p=e^{-rT}\left[K N(-d_2)-F N(-d_1)\right],
\]
\[
d_1=\frac{\ln(F/K)+\tfrac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},
\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{T}.
\]


Code
def normal_cdf(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    return 0.5 * (1 + np.vectorize(math.erf)(x / np.sqrt(2)))

def black_futures_put(F, K, T, r, sigma):
    vol_time = sigma * np.sqrt(T)
    d1 = (np.log(F / K) + 0.5 * sigma**2 * T) / vol_time
    d2 = d1 - vol_time
    return np.exp(-r * T) * (K * normal_cdf(-d2) - F * normal_cdf(-d1))

model_put_points = float(black_futures_put(futures_price, strike, time_to_expiry,
                                           risk_free_rate, volatility))
intrinsic_points = max(strike - futures_price, 0)
time_value_points = model_put_points - intrinsic_points

pd.Series({
    "Black put value (points)": model_put_points,
    "Black put value ($/contract)": model_put_points * dollars_per_point,
    "Intrinsic value (points)": intrinsic_points,
    "Time value (points)": time_value_points,
    "Illustrative quoted premium (points)": quoted_points,
}).round(4)

The quoted premium and model value need not match. A trader can interpret their difference as a signal to investigate volatility, exercise style, liquidity, model inputs, and bid-ask effects—not as an automatic arbitrage.

4 Size the Protective Put Overlay
First map the portfolio into futures-equivalent contracts:
\[
N_{fut-eq}=\frac{DV01_{portfolio}}{DV01_{futures}}.
\]
For a one-for-one static floor at expiration, buy approximately one put per futures-equivalent contract. A current delta hedge would generally require a different count and rebalancing.


Code

contracts = int(np.rint(exact_futures_equivalents))
premium_cost = contracts * quoted_dollars
mapped_dv01 = contracts * futures_dv01
residual_dv01 = portfolio_dv01 - mapped_dv01

pd.Series({
    "Exact futures equivalents": exact_futures_equivalents,
    "Static puts purchased": contracts,
    "Premium cost ($)": premium_cost,

}).round(2)

5 Futures-Price and Yield Scenarios
Approximate the futures-price change from a Treasury yield shock:
\[
\Delta F\approx-\frac{DV01_{futures}}{\$1{,}000\text{ per point}}\Delta y_{bp}.
\]
The mapped bond P&L moves like a long futures position. The protective put pays only below the strike. A short-futures hedge offsets mapped price changes linearly in both directions.

title: Practical Demo: Hedging with Options on Treasury Futures
text:
6 Risks the Simple Comparison Omits

Basis risk: the bond portfolio and Treasury futures may move differently.
Curve risk: a single contract cannot hedge every maturity exposure.
Volatility risk: option value changes when implied volatility changes.
Time decay: the put loses time value as expiration approaches, all else equal.
Delta drift: the option’s sensitivity changes with price, time, and volatility.
Exercise and margin conventions: listed contracts can differ from the European, premium-paid simplification.
Liquidity and roll risk: bid-ask costs and hedge replacement affect realized results.

title: Practical Demo: Hedging with Options on Treasury Futures
text:
8 Financial Interpretation
Contract selection begins with the risk, not the forecast. A short futures hedge is appropriate when the objective is to remove exposure linearly. A protective put is appropriate when the manager wants a loss floor while retaining favorable bond-price gains. That asymmetry is valuable, but its premium, volatility exposure, time decay, basis, and expiration must be budgeted explicitly.

Explain why the manager should compare the risk reduction with transaction cost.

Explain why rebalancing should not automatically eliminate every active view.

text: These 24 numerical and analytical problems review Lectures 1–6. Four problems are provided for each lecture. Attempt each problem before opening its solution. Keep rates in decimal form during calculations and state monetary units.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text: These 24 numerical and analytical problems review Lectures 1–6. Four problems are provided for each lecture. Attempt each problem before opening its solution. Keep rates in decimal form during calculations and state monetary units.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 1.1 Problem 1: Mapping a Bond’s Cash Flows
text:
1.1 Problem 1: Mapping a Bond’s Cash Flows
A corporation issues a $1,000 par, 6.40% annual-coupon bond with five years to maturity. Coupons are paid semiannually.

Compute the semiannual coupon and number of remaining payments.

List the cash flows received in periods 1, 9, and 10.

Compute total contractual cash flow over the bond’s remaining life.

Identify the issuer’s and investor’s obligations.







NoteSolution





The semiannual coupon is
\[C=1{,}000\left(\frac{0.064}{2}\right)=\boxed{\$32},\]
and there are \(5(2)=\boxed{10}\) payments. Periods 1 and 9 each pay $32; period 10 pays \(32+1{,}000=\$1{,}032\). Total contractual cash flow is
\[10(32)+1{,}000=\boxed{\$1{,}320}.\]
The issuer must make the promised coupons and repay principal, subject to default. The investor supplies the purchase price and receives the contractual cash flows. Total cash flow is not value because its components arrive at different dates.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
1.2 Problem 2: A Partially Amortizing Bond
A $10 million loan has a 5% annual coupon and repays $2 million of principal at each year-end for five years. Interest is computed on beginning-of-year principal.

Compute interest and total debt service in years 1 and 2.

Compute year-5 debt service.

Compute total interest over the loan’s life.

Contrast its principal profile with that of a bullet bond.







NoteSolution





Beginning principal is $10 million in year 1 and $8 million in year 2. Therefore,
\[I_1=0.05(10)=\$0.50\text{ million},\qquad
I_2=0.05(8)=\$0.40\text{ million}.\]
Adding the $2 million amortization gives debt service of $2.50 million and $2.40 million. In year 5, beginning principal is $2 million, so debt service is \(0.10+2.00=\boxed{\$2.10\text{ million}}\). Total interest is
\[0.05(10+8+6+4+2)=\boxed{\$1.50\text{ million}}.\]
A bullet bond repays all principal at maturity. Amortization returns principal earlier, reducing later interest and interest-rate exposure.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 1.3 Problem 3: Inflation and Realized Purchasing Power
text:
1.3 Problem 3: Inflation and Realized Purchasing Power
An investor buys a one-year zero-coupon bond for $950 and receives $1,000 at maturity. Inflation over the year is 3.25%.

Compute the nominal holding-period return.

Compute the exact real return.

Compute the maturity payment in beginning-of-year dollars.

Name two other risks that this calculation ignores.







NoteSolution





The nominal return is
\[R_n=\frac{1{,}000}{950}-1=\boxed{5.2632\%}.\]
The Fisher relation gives
\[R_r=\frac{1+R_n}{1+0.0325}-1
=\frac{1.052632}{1.0325}-1=\boxed{1.9498\%}.\]
The maturity payment has beginning-of-year purchasing power
\[\frac{1{,}000}{1.0325}=\boxed{\$968.52}.\]
The calculation ignores risks such as issuer default, liquidity, reinvestment, exchange-rate, call, and interim price risk.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
1.4 Problem 4: Call Risk and Reinvestment
A five-year, $1,000 par bond pays an 8% annual coupon and is callable at $1,020 immediately after the year-2 coupon. Just after issuance, comparable yields fall to 4%.

Compute the value at year 2 of the remaining three coupon-and-principal cash flows if the bond is not called.

Determine whether calling is economically attractive to the issuer.

Compute the investor’s year-2 cash flow if the bond is called.

Explain the investor’s reinvestment problem.







NoteSolution





Immediately after the year-2 coupon, the value of the remaining cash flows is
\[P_2=80\left(\frac{1-(1.04)^{-3}}{0.04}\right)
+1{,}000(1.04)^{-3}=\boxed{\$1{,}111.00}.\]
Redeeming at $1,020 rather than leaving debt worth about $1,111 outstanding is economically attractive, so exercise is likely. At year 2 the investor receives the $80 coupon plus $1,020 call price, or \(\boxed{\$1{,}100}\). The principal is returned precisely when market yields are low, so replacing the 8% coupon with an equally risky investment is difficult. This is call and reinvestment risk.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 2.1 Problem 5: Present Value and an Annuity
text:
2.1 Problem 5: Present Value and an Annuity
An investor will receive $4,000 at each year-end for four years and an additional $20,000 with the fourth payment. The annual discount rate is 6%.

Compute the present value of the four-payment annuity.

Compute the present value of the terminal amount.

Compute total present value.

Explain why discounting the total $36,000 for four years is incorrect.







NoteSolution





The annuity value is
\[PV_A=4{,}000\left(\frac{1-(1.06)^{-4}}{0.06}\right)
=\boxed{\$13{,}860.42}.\]
The terminal amount is worth
\[PV_F=20{,}000(1.06)^{-4}=\boxed{\$15{,}841.87}.\]
Thus total present value is \(\boxed{\$29{,}702.29}\). Discounting $36,000 for four years would incorrectly place the first three $4,000 payments at year 4.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 2.2 Problem 6: Pricing a Semiannual Coupon Bond
text:
2.2 Problem 6: Pricing a Semiannual Coupon Bond
A $1,000 par bond has a 5% annual coupon, six years to maturity, and a 6.20% yield to maturity quoted with semiannual compounding.

Identify the periodic coupon, periodic yield, and number of periods.

Compute the bond price.

State whether it trades at a premium or discount and why.

Compute its current yield.







NoteSolution





The inputs are \(C=\$25\), \(i=0.062/2=0.031\), and \(n=12\). Hence,
\[P=25\left(\frac{1-(1.031)^{-12}}{0.031}\right)
+1{,}000(1.031)^{-12}=\boxed{\$940.63}.\]
It trades at a discount because its 5% coupon rate is below the required 6.20% yield. Its current yield is
\[\frac{50}{940.63}=\boxed{5.3156\%}.\]
Current yield ignores capital gain and the timing and reinvestment of coupons.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 2.3 Problem 7: Clean Price, Accrued Interest, and Invoice Price
text:
2.3 Problem 7: Clean Price, Accrued Interest, and Invoice Price
A $1,000 par bond with a 7.20% annual coupon pays semiannually. Settlement occurs 73 days into a 182-day coupon period. The quoted clean price is 101.375% of par.

Compute the semiannual coupon.

Compute accrued interest using the actual-period fraction.

Compute the clean price in dollars.

Compute the full (invoice) price.







NoteSolution





The coupon is \(1{,}000(0.072/2)=\$36\). Accrued interest is
\[AI=36\left(\frac{73}{182}\right)=\boxed{\$14.44}.\]
The clean price is \(1.01375(1{,}000)=\boxed{\$1{,}013.75}\). Therefore,
\[P_{full}=1{,}013.75+14.44=\boxed{\$1{,}028.19}.\]
The quoted price excludes accrued interest; the buyer pays the full price at settlement.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
2.4 Problem 8: Horizon Return and Reinvestment
A two-year, $1,000 par bond pays a 6% annual coupon and is bought for $985. The first coupon is reinvested for one year at 3%; the bond is held to maturity.

Compute the horizon value of the first coupon.

Compute total wealth at the two-year horizon.

Compute the two-year holding-period return.

Compute the annualized compound return.







NoteSolution





The first coupon grows to
\[60(1.03)=\boxed{\$61.80}.\]
At maturity the second coupon and principal provide $1,060, so horizon wealth is \(1,121.80\). The two-year holding-period return is
\[\frac{1{,}121.80}{985}-1=\boxed{13.8883\%}.\]
The annualized return is
\[\left(\frac{1{,}121.80}{985}\right)^{1/2}-1=\boxed{6.7185\%}.\]
The result depends on the realized coupon reinvestment rate; YTM embeds a specific reinvestment assumption.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 3.1 Problem 9: Price Value of a Basis Point
text:
3.1 Problem 9: Price Value of a Basis Point
A bond is worth 103.18 when its yield is 4.99% and 103.02 when its yield is 5.01%. Its face amount is $5 million.

Estimate PVBP per $100 face value using a central difference.

Estimate modified duration using the midpoint price of 103.10.

Compute position DV01.

Estimate the loss for a 12 bp yield rise using duration only.







NoteSolution





The 2 bp price difference is $0.16, so the one-basis-point price value is
\[PVBP=\frac{103.18-103.02}{2}=\boxed{0.08\text{ per }\$100}.\]
Since \(PVBP\approx D_{mod}P(0.0001)\),
\[D_{mod}=\frac{0.08}{103.10(0.0001)}=\boxed{7.7595}.\]
There are \(5{,}000{,}000/100=50{,}000\) units, so position DV01 is \(0.08(50{,}000)=\boxed{\$4{,}000}\). A 12 bp rise produces an estimated loss of \(12(\$4{,}000)=\boxed{\$48{,}000}\).

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
3.2 Problem 10: Duration and Convexity Approximation
A bond has price 96.50, modified duration 6.40, and convexity 52. Its yield rises by 75 bps.

Compute the duration-only percentage price change.

Compute the convexity adjustment.

Compute the combined percentage and dollar price changes.

Explain the sign of the convexity term.







NoteSolution





With \(\Delta y=0.0075\),
\[\frac{\Delta P}{P}\bigg|_D=-6.40(0.0075)=\boxed{-4.8000\%}.\]
The convexity adjustment is
\[\frac{1}{2}(52)(0.0075)^2=\boxed{0.14625\%}.\]
Thus, \(\Delta P/P\approx-4.65375\%\) and
\[\Delta P=96.50(-0.0465375)=\boxed{-4.4909},\]
giving an estimated price of 92.0091. For an option-free bond with positive convexity, curvature raises the price relative to the tangent-line estimate for either direction of the yield change.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 3.3 Problem 11: Portfolio Duration and a Hedge
text:
3.3 Problem 11: Portfolio Duration and a Hedge
A $20 million portfolio holds 30% in a duration-2.0 bond, 45% in a duration-6.0 bond, and 25% in a duration-10.0 bond. A Treasury futures contract has DV01 $82.

Compute portfolio modified duration.

Compute portfolio DV01.

Compute the number of contracts for a duration hedge.

State the appropriate futures position for hedging a long bond portfolio.







NoteSolution





Market-value-weighted duration is
\[D_P=0.30(2.0)+0.45(6.0)+0.25(10.0)=\boxed{5.80}.\]
Therefore,
\[DV01_P=20{,}000{,}000(5.80)(0.0001)=\boxed{\$11{,}600}.\]
The hedge requires
\[N=\frac{11{,}600}{82}=141.46,\]
or about \(\boxed{141\text{ or }142}\) contracts depending on the desired rounding. The portfolio should short futures because a rate rise lowers both the bonds and, typically, the futures price.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
3.4 Problem 12: Key-Rate Duration Exposure
A $12 million portfolio has 2-year, 5-year, and 10-year key-rate durations of 0.80, 3.10, and 2.40. The corresponding key rates change by +15, -5, and +20 bps.

Compute the first-order percentage price contribution from each key rate.

Compute the total estimated percentage price change.

Compute the dollar price change.

Explain why total duration alone cannot reproduce every such scenario.







NoteSolution





Using \(\Delta P/P\approx-\sum_i KRD_i\Delta y_i\), the contributions are
\[-0.80(0.0015)=-0.1200\%,\]
\[-3.10(-0.0005)=+0.1550\%,\]
\[-2.40(0.0020)=-0.4800\%.\]
The total is \(\boxed{-0.4450\%}\), giving
\[\Delta P=12{,}000{,}000(-0.00445)=\boxed{-\$53{,}400}.\]
Total duration collapses curve exposure into one parallel-shift measure. Key-rate durations retain information about where the curve moves.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 4.1 Problem 13: Yield Decomposition and Spread Change
text:
4.1 Problem 13: Yield Decomposition and Spread Change
A five-year corporate bond yields 6.35% when the matched Treasury yields 4.60%. One month later, the corporate yield is 6.10% and the Treasury yield is 4.20%.

Compute the initial benchmark spread.

Compute the new benchmark spread.

Decompose the corporate yield change into base-rate and spread changes.

Interpret the spread movement.







NoteSolution





Initially,
\[s_0=6.35\%-4.60\%=\boxed{175\text{ bps}}.\]
The new spread is \(6.10\%-4.20\%=\boxed{190\text{ bps}}\). The Treasury base rate fell 40 bps while the spread widened 15 bps, producing a net corporate yield change of \(-40+15=\boxed{-25\text{ bps}}\). The wider spread indicates weaker relative valuation, liquidity, or perceived credit quality even though the bond’s all-in yield declined.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
4.2 Problem 14: Bootstrapping Spot Rates
One-year and two-year annual-pay par Treasury securities have coupon rates of 4.00% and 5.00%, respectively. Both have par value 100.

Compute the one-year spot rate.

Write the two-year par-bond pricing equation.

Bootstrap the two-year spot rate.

Price a two-year zero-coupon Treasury with face value $1,000.







NoteSolution





The one-year par security implies \(z_1=\boxed{4.00\%}\). For the two-year bond,
\[100=\frac{5}{1.04}+\frac{105}{(1+z_2)^2}.\]
Thus,
\[(1+z_2)^2=\frac{105}{100-5/1.04}=1.10303,\]
so \(z_2=\boxed{5.0253\%}\). The zero’s price is
\[P_0=\frac{1{,}000}{(1.050253)^2}=\boxed{\$906.59}.\]
Each cash flow is discounted at the spot rate matching its date.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
4.3 Problem 15: An Implied Forward Rate
The one-year spot rate is 3.20% and the two-year spot rate is 4.10%, with annual compounding.

Compute the one-year forward rate one year from now.

Verify the result by comparing two-year growth factors.

Compute the forward rate if the two-year spot rate instead equals 3.00%.

Explain what an implied forward rate is and is not.







NoteSolution





No-arbitrage requires
\[(1+z_2)^2=(1+z_1)(1+f_{1,1}).\]
Therefore,
\[f_{1,1}=\frac{(1.041)^2}{1.032}-1=\boxed{5.0078\%}.\]
Indeed, \((1.032)(1.050078)=(1.041)^2\). If \(z_2=3.00\%\),
\[f_{1,1}=\frac{(1.03)^2}{1.032}-1=\boxed{2.8004\%}.\]
The forward rate is the future borrowing/lending rate locked in by current spot prices. It is not necessarily an unbiased forecast of the future spot rate because risk premiums and other effects may matter.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
4.4 Problem 16: A Duration-Neutral Curve Trade
A manager expects the 10-year yield to fall relative to the 2-year yield. A $4 million long 10-year position has modified duration 8.20. The 2-year bond used for the short hedge has modified duration 1.85.

Compute the long position’s DV01.

Find the market value of the 2-year short position that makes parallel DV01 approximately neutral.

If the 10-year yield falls 12 bps and the 2-year yield falls 4 bps, estimate the trade’s P&L.

Identify one residual risk.







NoteSolution





The long position’s DV01 is
\[4{,}000{,}000(8.20)(0.0001)=\boxed{\$3{,}280}.\]
Set the short bond’s DV01 equal to $3,280:
\[MV_S=\frac{3{,}280}{1.85(0.0001)}=\boxed{\$17.7297\text{ million}}.\]
The long gains \(12(3,280)=\$39,360\). The short loses \(4(3,280)=\$13,120\), so net P&L is \(\boxed{\$26,240}\). Residual risks include convexity, imperfect key-rate mapping, financing, liquidity, and spread changes.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
5.1 Problem 17: Treasury Bill Pricing
A 182-day Treasury bill has face value $1,000,000 and a bank discount yield of 4.80%. Use a 360-day year for the discount quotation.

Compute the dollar discount.

Compute the purchase price.

Compute the holding-period yield.

Compute the bond-equivalent yield using a 365-day year.







NoteSolution





The dollar discount is
\[D=1{,}000{,}000(0.048)\left(\frac{182}{360}\right)
=\boxed{\$24{,}266.67}.\]
Price is \(\boxed{\$975{,}733.33}\). The holding-period yield is
\[HPY=\frac{24{,}266.67}{975{,}733.33}=\boxed{2.4870\%}.\]
The simple bond-equivalent yield is
\[BEY=HPY\left(\frac{365}{182}\right)=\boxed{4.9877\%}.\]
The bank discount yield divides by face value and uses a 360-day year, so it is not directly comparable with a price-based investment yield.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
5.2 Problem 18: Treasury Auction Allocation
At a Treasury auction, $30 billion is offered. Noncompetitive tenders total $2 billion. Competitive bids at or below the stop-out yield total $35 billion.

How much remains for competitive bidders?

Compute the competitive allocation percentage.

Find the allocation to a successful $500 million competitive bid.

State the pricing implication of a single-price auction.







NoteSolution





After noncompetitive awards, competitive bidders can receive
\[30-2=\boxed{\$28\text{ billion}}.\]
The pro rata allocation percentage is
\[\frac{28}{35}=\boxed{80\%}.\]
A successful $500 million bid receives \(500(0.80)=\boxed{\$400\text{ million}}\). In a single-price auction, accepted competitive and noncompetitive awards receive the price corresponding to the stop-out yield, rather than each bidder’s submitted yield.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 5.3 Problem 19: Expected Credit Loss and Recovery
text:
5.3 Problem 19: Expected Credit Loss and Recovery
A one-year corporate note has $8 million face value, a 2.5% probability of default, and a 40% recovery rate on face value if default occurs. Ignore coupons and discounting.

Compute loss given default in dollars.

Compute expected credit loss.

Compute the expected maturity principal payment.

Recompute expected loss if recovery falls to 25%.







NoteSolution





Loss given default is
\[LGD=8{,}000{,}000(1-0.40)=\boxed{\$4{,}800{,}000}.\]
Expected loss is
\[EL=0.025(4{,}800{,}000)=\boxed{\$120{,}000}.\]
Expected principal is \(8{,}000{,}000-120{,}000=\boxed{\$7{,}880{,}000}\). At 25% recovery, expected loss becomes
\[0.025[8{,}000{,}000(0.75)]=\boxed{\$150{,}000}.\]
Expected loss combines default probability, exposure, and loss severity; it does not describe unexpected loss or mark-to-market spread volatility.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
5.4 Problem 20: Commercial Paper Funding Cost
A company issues $25 million face value of 90-day commercial paper at a price of 99.10% of face value. Ignore issuance fees.

Compute cash proceeds.

Compute dollar interest cost.

Compute the 90-day holding-period yield to the investor.

Annualize that yield on a simple 360-day basis and identify the main credit feature of commercial paper.







NoteSolution





The issuer receives
\[25{,}000{,}000(0.991)=\boxed{\$24{,}775{,}000}.\]
Dollar interest is \(25{,}000{,}000-24{,}775{,}000=\boxed{\$225{,}000}\). The investor’s holding-period yield is
\[HPY=\frac{225{,}000}{24{,}775{,}000}=\boxed{0.9082\%}.\]
The simple annualized yield is \(0.9082\%(360/90)=\boxed{3.6327\%}\). Commercial paper is an unsecured short-term corporate obligation, so repayment depends on the issuer’s credit and liquidity access.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
6.1 Problem 21: Two-Asset Portfolio Risk
A portfolio invests 60% in Bond A and 40% in Bond B. Annual return volatilities are 5% and 8%, and their correlation is 0.25. Expected returns are 4% and 6%.

Compute expected portfolio return.

Compute portfolio variance.

Compute portfolio volatility.

Compare it with the weighted average volatility and explain the difference.







NoteSolution





Expected return is
\[E[R_P]=0.60(0.04)+0.40(0.06)=\boxed{4.80\%}.\]
Variance is
\[\sigma_P^2=(0.60)^2(0.05)^2+(0.40)^2(0.08)^2
+2(0.60)(0.40)(0.25)(0.05)(0.08)=\boxed{0.002404}.\]
Thus \(\sigma_P=\sqrt{0.002404}=\boxed{4.9031\%}\). Weighted average volatility is \(0.60(5\%)+0.40(8\%)=6.20\%\). Portfolio risk is lower because imperfectly correlated returns provide diversification.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
6.2 Problem 22: Ex Post Tracking Error
A portfolio’s six monthly active returns, in basis points, are
\[12,\;-8,\;5,\;-3,\;10,\;-4.\]

Compute mean monthly active return.

Compute sample monthly tracking error.

Annualize tracking error using \(\sqrt{12}\).

Explain what tracking error measures.







NoteSolution





The mean is
\[\bar{r}_A=\frac{12-8+5-3+10-4}{6}=\boxed{2\text{ bps}}.\]
Deviations are \(10,-10,3,-5,8,-6\), whose squared sum is 334. Therefore,
\[TE_m=\sqrt{\frac{334}{6-1}}=\boxed{8.1731\text{ bps per month}}.\]
Annualized tracking error is
\[TE_a=8.1731\sqrt{12}=\boxed{28.31\text{ bps per year}}.\]
Tracking error measures the variability of returns relative to a benchmark, not the portfolio’s total return volatility or average active return.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
text:
6.3 Problem 23: Cell-Based Sampling
A benchmark and a sampled portfolio have the following weights:



Cell
Benchmark
Portfolio
Cell duration




Treasury 1–3 year
25%
20%
1.9


Treasury 7–10 year
30%
35%
7.8


Corporate 1–3 year
20%
25%
2.1


Corporate 7–10 year
25%
20%
7.2




Compute each active cell weight.

Verify that active weights sum to zero.

Compute benchmark and portfolio duration.

Identify the portfolio’s principal sector and curve tilts.







NoteSolution





Portfolio minus benchmark active weights are
\[\boxed{-5\%,\quad+5\%,\quad+5\%,\quad-5\%},\]
which sum to zero. Benchmark duration is
\[D_B=0.25(1.9)+0.30(7.8)+0.20(2.1)+0.25(7.2)=\boxed{5.035}.\]
Portfolio duration is
\[D_P=0.20(1.9)+0.35(7.8)+0.25(2.1)+0.20(7.2)=\boxed{5.075}.\]
The portfolio overweights long Treasuries and short corporates while underweighting short Treasuries and long corporates. Its net duration is only 0.040 above the benchmark, showing that similar aggregate duration can conceal meaningful cell tilts.

title: Practice Problems 1: Lectures 1–6
section: 6.4 Problem 24: Factor Tracking Error and Risk Contribution
text:
6.4 Problem 24: Factor Tracking Error and Risk Contribution
A portfolio has active exposure 0.20 to a level factor and \(-0.15\) to a spread factor. Annual factor volatilities are 4% and 6%, their correlation is 0.30, and annual idiosyncratic tracking-error volatility is 0.50%.

Compute the level-factor variance contribution.

Compute the spread-factor variance contribution and covariance term.

Compute total tracking-error variance and volatility.

Explain one way the manager could reduce predicted tracking error.







NoteSolution





Let active exposures be \(b_L=0.20\) and \(b_S=-0.15\). The diagonal contributions are
\[b_L^2\sigma_L^2=(0.20)^2(0.04)^2=0.000064,\]
\[b_S^2\sigma_S^2=(-0.15)^2(0.06)^2=0.000081.\]
The covariance term is
\[2b_Lb_S\rho\sigma_L\sigma_S
=2(0.20)(-0.15)(0.30)(0.04)(0.06)=-0.0000432.\]
Adding idiosyncratic variance, \((0.005)^2=0.000025\), gives
\[TE^2=0.000064+0.000081-0.0000432+0.000025
=\boxed{0.0001268},\]
so \(TE=\sqrt{0.0001268}=\boxed{1.1261\%}\). The manager can move factor exposures toward zero, substitute securities with better benchmark matching, or reduce idiosyncratic concentration, subject to return and transaction-cost objectives.
